heading: Retractatio
latin: In hoc Opusculo, cum illud de Evangelio, quod Dominus ait, diem ultimi iudicii se nescire, ad aliquam sententiam confirmandam atque corroborandam proferrem in medium (cap. 1, n. 1), improvide quidem apposui, quod in Evangelio scriptum non esse postea deprehendi. Nam cum textus habeat tantummodo, neque filius scit; ego deceptus magis, quam fallere volens, litterae quippe immemor, sed non sensus, «Nec ipse,» inquam, «Filius hominis scit.» Unde etiam totam ordiens sequentem disputationem, ex eo quod non veraciter posui, veram conatus sum approbare assertionem. Sed quia talem errorem meum multo post, quam a me idem libellus editus, et a pluribus iam transcriptus fuit, deprehendi; cum non potui per tot iam libellos sparsum persequi mendacium, necessarium credidi confugere ad confessionis remedium. Alio quoque in loco (Cap. 10, n. 35) quamdam de Seraphim opinionem posui, quam nunquam audivi, nusquam legi. Ubi sane lector meus attendat, quod proinde temperanter, «puto,» dixerim: volens videlicet non aliud, quam putari, quod certum reddere de Scripturis non valui. Titulus quoque ipse qui de Gradibus Humilitatis inscribitur, pro eo forsitan quod non humilitatis, sed superbiae potius hic distingui describique gradus videntur, calumniam patietur, sed hoc a minus vel intelligentibus, vel attendentibus eius tituli rationem, quam tamen in fine opusculi ipse breviter intimare curavi.
english: In this little work, when I brought forward that saying of the Gospel in which the Lord states that He does not know the day of the last judgment, in order to confirm and strengthen a certain opinion (ch. 1, n. 1), I incautiously added a word which I afterwards found is not written in the Gospel. For while the text has only “nor does the Son know,” I, misled rather than wishing to mislead, unmindful of the letter though not of the sense, wrote, “Nor does the Son of Man Himself know.” And from that inaccurate wording I then built the whole of the following argument, trying to prove a true claim from something I had not truly set down. But because I discovered this error of mine long after the booklet had been published by me and already copied by many, and I could not chase a falsehood already scattered through so many copies, I thought it necessary to take refuge in the remedy of confession. In another place also (ch. 10, n. 35) I set down an opinion about the Seraphim which I have never heard and nowhere read. Here my reader should notice that I therefore said, with restraint, “I suppose”: meaning that I wished nothing more than that it be taken as a conjecture, since I could not make it certain from the Scriptures. The title itself, which is inscribed “On the Steps of Humility,” may also meet with censure, perhaps because the steps distinguished and described here seem to be those of pride rather than of humility; but this will come only from those who understand or attend too little to the reason of that title, which I have been careful to indicate briefly at the end of the work.
label: Retractatio

heading: Praefatio
latin: Rogasti me, frater Godefride, ut ea quae de gradibus humilitatis coram fratribus locutus fueram, pleniori tibi tractatu dissererem. Cui tuae petitioni digne, ut dignum erat, et volens satisfacere, et timens non posse, evangelici consilii memor, non prius, fateor, incipere ausus sum, quam sedens computavi, si sufficerent sumptus ad perficiendum (Luc. XIV, 28). Cum autem caritas hunc foras misisset timorem, quo mihi timebam illudi de opere non consummando, subintravit alius timor de contrario, quo coepi timere gravius periculum de gloria si perfecissem, quam de ignominia si defecissem. Unde inter hunc timorem et caritatem, velut in quodam bivio positus, diu haesitavi, cui viarum tuto me crederem; metuens aut loquendo utiliter de humilitate, ipse humilis non inveniri; aut tacendo humiliter, inutilis fieri. Cumque neutram viam tutam, alterutram tamen mihi tenendam esse conspicerem; elegi potius tibi, si quem possem, communicare fructum sermonis, quam tutari me solum portu silentii: simul fiduciam habens, si quid forte, quod approbes, dixerim, tuis precibus posse me non superbire; sin autem (quod magis puto) nihil tuo studio dignum effecerim, de nihilo superbire non posse.
english: You asked me, brother Godfrey, to set out more fully, in a treatise for you, those things I had spoken before the brothers concerning the steps of humility. Wishing to satisfy this request of yours as it deserved, and fearing that I could not, and mindful of the Gospel counsel, I confess that I did not dare to begin until I had sat down and counted whether I had resources enough to finish (Luke 14:28). Then, when charity had cast out this fear—the fear of being mocked for a work left unfinished—another fear of the opposite kind came in, and I began to dread a graver danger from glory if I succeeded than from disgrace if I failed. And so, placed as it were at a fork between this fear and charity, I hesitated long as to which road I might safely trust; fearing either that, by speaking usefully of humility, I myself might be found not humble, or that, by keeping a humble silence, I might become useless. And since I saw that neither way was safe, yet that I must take one of them, I chose rather to share with you, if I could, the fruit of the discourse, than to keep myself alone in the harbor of silence: trusting at the same time that if I should happen to say something you approve, I may by your prayers be kept from pride; but if (as I rather think) I produce nothing worthy of your study, I cannot be proud of nothing.

heading: CAPUT PRIMUM. Christum esse viam humilitatis, qua pervenitur ad veritatem
latin: CAPUT PRIMUM. Christum esse viam humilitatis, qua pervenitur ad veritatem.
english: Chapter I. That Christ is the way of humility by which one comes to the truth.
label: CAPUT PRIMUM. Christum esse viam humilitatis, qua pervenitur ad veritatem

chunks.latin: CAPUT PRIMUM. Christum esse viam humilitatis, qua pervenitur ad veritatem.
chunks.english: Chapter I. That Christ is the way of humility by which one comes to the truth.

latin: Locuturus ergo de gradibus humilitatis, quos beatus Benedictus non numerandos, sed ascendendos proponit (Reg. cap. 7), prius ostendo, si possum, quo per illos perveniendum sit, ut audito fructu perventionis, minus gravet labor ascensionis. Proponit itaque Dominus nobis viae laborem, laboris mercedem Ego sum, inquit, via, veritas, et vita (Ioan. XIV, 6). Viam dicit humilitatem, quae ducit ad veritatem. Altera labor, altera fructus laboris est. Unde sciam, inquis, quod ibi de humilitate locutus sit, cum indeterminate dixerit: Ego sum via? Audi apertius: Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Matth. XI. 29). Se ergo proponit humilitatis exemplum, mansuetudinis formam. Si imitaris eum, non ambulas in tenebris, sed habebis lumen vitae (Ioan. VIII, 12). Quid est lumen vitae, nisi veritas; quae illuminans omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, ostendit ubi sit vera vita? Ideo cum dixisset, Ego sum via et veritas, subdidit, et vita: ac si diceret: Ego sum via, quae ad veritatem duco; ego sum veritas quae vitam promitto: ego sum vita, quam do. Haec est enim, ait, vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum: et quem misisti Iesum Christum (Matth. XVII, 3). Vel sic, quasi tu dicas: Viam considero, id est humilitatem: fructum desidero, veritatem. Sed quid si tantus est labor viae, ut ad optatum lucrum non possim pervenire? Respondet: Ego sum via, id est viaticum, quo sustenteris in via. Clamat igitur errantibus, et viam ignorantibus, Ego sum via: dubitantibus, et non credentibus, Ego sum veritas: iam ascendentibus, sed lassescentibus, Ego sum vita. Satis, ut reor, ostensum est ex proposito capitulo Evangelii, cognitionem veritatis fructum esse humilitatis. Accipe et aliud. Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine coeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec, haud dubium quin veritatis secreta, a sapientibus et prudentibus, id est a superbis, et revelasti ea parvulis (Luc. X, 21), hoc est humilibus. Et in hoc apparet quod veritas, quae superbis absconditur, humilibus revelatur.
english: About to speak, then, of the steps of humility, which blessed Benedict sets before us not to be numbered but to be climbed (Rule, ch. 7), I first show, if I can, whither one must come by them, so that when the fruit of arrival is heard, the labor of the ascent may weigh less. So the Lord sets before us the labor of the way and the reward of the labor: “I am,” He says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He calls the way humility, which leads to the truth. The one is labor, the other the fruit of labor. “How am I to know,” you ask, “that He was speaking there of humility, when He said indefinitely, ‘I am the way’?” Hear more plainly: “Learn from Me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He therefore sets Himself forth as the example of humility, the pattern of meekness. If you imitate Him, you do not walk in darkness, but you will have the light of life (John 8:12). What is the light of life, if not the truth, which, enlightening every man coming into this world, shows where true life is? Therefore when He had said, “I am the way and the truth,” He added, “and the life”: as if He said, “I am the way, who lead to the truth; I am the truth, who promise life; I am the life, which I give.” “For this,” He says, “is eternal life, that they may know You, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.” Or thus, as if you should say: “I consider the way, that is humility; I desire the fruit, the truth. But what if the labor of the way is so great that I cannot reach the hoped-for gain?” He answers: “I am the life,” that is, the provision by which you may be sustained on the way. He therefore cries to those who wander and do not know the way, “I am the way”; to those who doubt and do not believe, “I am the truth”; to those already climbing but growing weary, “I am the life.” Enough, I think, has been shown from the proposed chapter of the Gospel, that the knowledge of the truth is the fruit of humility. Take another saying also. “I confess to You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things”—no doubt the secrets of the truth—“from the wise and prudent,” that is, from the proud, “and have revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21), that is, to the humble. And in this it appears that the truth, which is hidden from the proud, is revealed to the humble.

latin: Humilitatis vero talis potest esse definitio: Humilitas est virtus, qua homo verissima sui agnitione sibi ipsi vilescit. Haec autem convenit his qui ascensionibus in corde suo dispositis, de virtute in virtutem, id est de gradu in gradum proficiunt, donec ad culmen humilitatis perveniant, in quo velut in Sion, id est in speculatione, positi, veritatem prospiciant. Etenim, inquit, benedictionem dabit legislator (Psal. LXXXIII, 8): quia qui dedit legem, dabit et benedictionem; hoc est, qui iussit humilitatem, perducet ad veritatem. Quis vero est hic legislator, nisi dulcis et rectus Dominus qui legem dedit delinquentibus in via? (Psal. XXIV, 8.) In via quippe delinquunt, qui veritatem derelinquunt. Sed nunquid vel sic a dulci Domino derelinquuntur? Ipsis ergo dulcis et rectus Dominus legem dat viam humilitatis, per quam redeant ad cognitionem veritatis. Dat occasionem recuperandae salutis, quia dulcis est; non tamen absque disciplina legis, quia rectus est. Dulcis, quia perire non patitur; rectus, quia punire non obliviscitur.
english: Now such may be the definition of humility: Humility is the virtue by which a man, through a most true knowledge of himself, becomes cheap in his own eyes. This belongs to those who, having set ascents in their heart, advance from virtue to virtue, that is from step to step, until they come to the summit of humility, in which, placed as it were in Zion, that is in contemplation, they look upon the truth. For “the lawgiver,” it is said, “will give a blessing” (Ps. 83:8): because He who gave the law will also give the blessing; that is, He who commanded humility will lead through to the truth. And who is this lawgiver, if not the Lord, sweet and upright, who gave a law to those who go astray in the way? (Ps. 24:8.) They go astray in the way who abandon the truth. But are they even so abandoned by the sweet Lord? To them, then, the Lord, sweet and upright, gives as a law the way of humility, by which they may return to the knowledge of the truth. He gives an occasion of recovering salvation, because He is sweet; yet not without the discipline of the law, because He is upright. Sweet, because He does not suffer them to perish; upright, because He does not forget to punish.

heading: CAPUT II. Quo fructu ascendantur gradus humilitatis
latin: CAPUT II. Quo fructu ascendantur gradus humilitatis.
english: Chapter II. With what fruit the steps of humility are climbed.
label: CAPUT II. Quo fructu ascendantur gradus humilitatis

chunks.latin: CAPUT II. Quo fructu ascendantur gradus humilitatis.
chunks.english: Chapter II. With what fruit the steps of humility are climbed.

latin: Hanc itaque legem, qua reditur ad veritatem, beatus Benedictus per duodecim gradus disponit: ut sicut per decem praecepta legis ac geminam circumcisionem (in quo duodenarius numerus adimpletur) ad Christum venitur; ita his duodecim gradibus ascensis, veritas apprehendatur. Illud quoque quod in scala illa, quae in typo humilitatis Iacob monstrata est, Dominus desuper innixus apparuit (Gen. XXVIII, 12, 13), quid nobis aliud innuit, nisi quod in culmine humilitatis constituitur cognitio veritatis? Dominus quippe de summitate scalae prospiciebat super filios hominum tanquam Veritas, cuius oculi sicut fallere nolunt, ita falli non norunt, ut videret si est intelligens aut requirens Deum. An non tibi de alto videtur clamare ac dicere requirentibus se (novit enim qui sunt eius): Transite ad me, omnes qui concupiscitis me, et a generationibus meis implemini? (Eccli. XXIV, 26) et illud: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego vos reficiam (Matth. XI, 28). Venite, inquit. Quo? Ad me veritatem. Qua? Per humilitatem. Quo fructu? Ego vos reficiam. Sed quae est refectio, quam Veritas ascendentibus promittit, pervenientibus reddit? An forte ipsa est caritas? Ad hanc quippe, ut ait beatus Benedictus, ascensis omnibus humilitatis gradibus monachus mox perveniet (Reg. cap. 7, grad. 12). Vere dulcis et suavis cibus caritas, quae fessos allevat, debiles roborat, moestos laetificat. Iugum denique Veritatis facit suave, et onus leve.
english: This law, then, by which one returns to the truth, blessed Benedict arranges in twelve steps: so that as through the ten commandments of the Law and the twofold circumcision (in which the number twelve is completed) one comes to Christ, so when these twelve steps have been climbed, the truth is laid hold of. That also which appeared in that ladder shown to Jacob as a type of humility, the Lord leaning upon it from above (Gen. 28:12–13)—what else does it hint to us, except that the knowledge of the truth is set at the summit of humility? For the Lord looked down from the top of the ladder upon the children of men as Truth, whose eyes as they will not deceive, so they do not know how to be deceived, that He might see if there is one who understands or seeks God. Does He not seem to you to cry from on high and to say to those who seek Him (for He knows who are His): “Come over to Me, all you who desire Me, and be filled from my produce”? (Sir. 24:26) and this: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). “Come,” He says. Whither? To Me, the truth. By what way? Through humility. With what fruit? “I will refresh you.” But what is the refreshment which Truth promises to those who climb and pays to those who arrive? Is it perhaps charity itself? For to this, as blessed Benedict says, the monk will soon come when all the steps of humility have been climbed (Rule, ch. 7, step 12). Truly sweet and pleasant food is charity, which lifts the weary, strengthens the weak, gladdens the sad. In short, it makes the yoke of Truth sweet and its burden light.

latin: Bonus cibus caritas, quae media in ferculo Salomonis consistens (Cantic. III, 9, 10), diversarum odore virtutum, velut diversi generis fragrantia pigmentorum, esurientes reficit, iucundat reficientes. Ibi siquidem apponitur pax, patientia, benignitas, longanimitas, gaudium in Spiritu sancto: et si quae sunt aliae veritatis seu sapientiae generationes, apparantur in illa. Habet et humilitas in eodem ferculo suas epulas, panem scilicet doloris et vinum compunctionis, quas primo Veritas incipientibus offert, quibus utique dicitur: Surgite postquam sederitis, qui manducatis panem doloris (Psal. CXXVI, 2). Habet ibidem contemplatio ex adipe frumenti solidum cibum sapientiae, cum vino quod laetificat cor hominis, ad quae Veritas perfectos invitat, dicens: Comedite, amici mei, et bibite; et inebriamini, charissimi (Cantic. V, 1). Media, inquit, caritate constravit propter filias Ierusalem (id. II, 10); propter imperfectas videlicet animas, quae, dum adhuc illum solidum cibum minus capere possunt, lacte interim caritatis pro pane, oleo pro vino nutriendae sunt. Quae recte media describitur, quia eius suavitas nec incipientibus praesto est, prohibente timore; nec perfectis satis est, pro abundantiori contemplationis dulcedine. Hi adhuc a noxiis carnalium delectationum humoribus, timoris amarissima potione purgandi, nondum lactis dulcedinem experiuntur: illi iam avulsi a lacte, epulari ab introitu gloriae gloriosius delectantur: solis mediis, id est proficientibus, ita iam melleas quasdam sorbitiunculas caritatis expertis, ut illis interim pro sui teneritudine contenti sint.
english: Good food is charity, which, standing in the middle of Solomon’s litter (Song 3:9–10), by the scent of various virtues, as by the fragrance of spices of different kinds, refreshes the hungry and delights those who are refreshed. For there are set out peace, patience, kindness, long-suffering, joy in the Holy Spirit; and if there are any other fruits of truth or of wisdom, they are served in it. Humility also has its dishes in the same litter: namely the bread of sorrow and the wine of compunction, which Truth first offers to beginners, to whom it is said: “Rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:2). Contemplation has there, from the fat of wheat, the solid food of wisdom, with the wine that gladdens the heart of man, to which Truth invites the perfect, saying: “Eat, my friends, and drink; and be inebriated, O dearest” (Song 5:1). “He paved the middle,” it says, “with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem”; that is, for imperfect souls, who, while they still cannot take that solid food, must for a time be nourished with the milk of charity instead of bread, and with oil instead of wine. And it is rightly described as in the middle, because its sweetness is not yet at hand for beginners, fear forbidding it; nor is it enough for the perfect, on account of the more abundant sweetness of contemplation. The former, still to be purged by the most bitter drink of fear from the noxious humors of carnal delights, do not yet taste the sweetness of milk; the latter, already weaned from milk, are more gloriously delighted to feast from the entrance of glory: only those in the middle, that is those making progress, have already tasted certain honeyed sips of charity, so as for the time to be content with them because of their tenderness.

latin: Primus ergo cibus est humilitatis, purgatorius cum amaritudine: secundus caritatis, consolatorius cum dulcedine: tertius contemplationis, solidus cum fortitudine. Heu mihi, Domine Deus virtutum! quousque irasceris super orationem servi tui, cibabis me pane lacrymarum, et potum dabis mihi in lacrymis? Quis me invitabit ad illud vel medium ac dulce caritatis convivium: ubi iusti epulantur in conspectu Dei, et delectantur in laetitia, ut iam non loquens in amaritudine animae meae, dicam Deo, Noli me condemnare: sed epulando in azymis sinceritatis et veritatis, laetus cantem in viis Domini, quoniam magna est gloria Domini? Bona tamen via humilitatis, qua veritas inquiritur, caritas acquiritur, generationes sapientiae participantur. Denique sicut finis legis Christus, sic perfectio humilitatis, cognitio veritatis. Christus cum venit attulit gratiam: Veritas quibus innotuerit, dat caritatem. Innotescit autem humilibus: humilibus ergo dat gratiam.
english: The first food, then, is that of humility, purgative with bitterness; the second, of charity, consoling with sweetness; the third, of contemplation, solid with strength. Woe is me, O Lord God of hosts! How long will You be angry against the prayer of Your servant, and feed me with the bread of tears, and give me tears to drink? Who will invite me even to that middle and sweet banquet of charity, where the just feast in the sight of God and delight in gladness, so that I may no longer speak in the bitterness of my soul and say to God, “Do not condemn me,” but, feasting on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, may sing gladly in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord? Yet good is the way of humility, by which truth is sought, charity is gained, and the fruits of wisdom are shared. In short, as the end of the law is Christ, so the perfection of humility is the knowledge of the truth. Christ, when He came, brought grace: Truth, to those to whom it becomes known, gives charity. But it becomes known to the humble: therefore it is to the humble that it gives grace.

heading: CAPUT III. Quo ordine gradus humilitatis ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant: et quomodo Christus per passionem didicit misericordiam
latin: CAPUT III. Quo ordine gradus humilitatis ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant: et quomodo Christus per passionem didicit misericordiam.
english: Chapter III. In what order the steps of humility lead to the appointed prize of truth; and how Christ learned mercy through His Passion.
label: CAPUT III. Quo ordine gradus humilitatis ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant: et quomodo Christus per passionem didicit misericordiam

chunks.latin: CAPUT III. Quo ordine gradus humilitatis ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant: et quomodo Christus per passionem didicit misericordiam.
chunks.english: Chapter III. In what order the steps of humility lead to the appointed prize of truth; and how Christ learned mercy through His Passion.

latin: Dixi, ut potui, quo fructu humilitatis gradus ascendi debeant: dicam, ut potero, quo ordine ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant. Sed, quia ipsa quoque veritatis agnitio in tribus gradibus consistit, ipsos breviter, si possum, distinguo: quatenus ex hoc clarius innotescat, ad quem trium veritatis, duodecimus humilitatis pertingat. Inquirimus namque veritatem in nobis, in proximis, in sui natura. In nobis, nosmetipsos diiudicando: in proximis, eorum malis compatiendo: in sui natura mundo corde contemplando. Observa sicut numerum, ita et ordinem. Primo te doceat Veritas ipsa, quod prius in proximis quam in sui debeat inquiri natura. Post hoc accipies, cur prius in te, quam in proximis inquirere debeas. In numero siquidem beatitudinum, quas suo sermone distinxit Dominus, prius misericordes, quam mundicordes posuit (Matth. V, 7, 8). Misericordes quippe cito in proximis veritatem deprehendunt, dum suos affectus in illos extendunt: dum sic per caritatem se illis conformant, ut illorum vel bona, vel mala, tanquam propria sentiant. Cum infirmis infirmantur, cum scandalizatis uruntur (II Cor. XI, 29). Gaudere cum gaudentibus, flere cum flentibus consueverunt (Rom. XII, 15). Hac caritate fraterna cordis acie mundata, veritatem delectantur in sui contemplari 362 natura, pro cuius amore mala tolerant aliena. Qui vero ita se fratribus non consociant, sed e contrario aut flentibus insultant, aut gaudentibus derogant, dum quod in illis est, in se esse non sentiunt, quia similiter affecti non sunt, veritatem in proximis qualiter deprehendere possunt? Bene namque convenit illis illud vulgare proverbium: Nescit sanus quid sentiat aeger, aut plenus quid patiatur ieiunus. Et aeger aegro, et ieiunus ieiuno quanto propinquius, tanto familiarius compatiuntur. Sicut enim pura veritas non nisi puro corde videtur; sic miseria fratris verius misero corde sentitur. Sed ut ob alienam miseriam miserum cor habeas, oportet ut tuam prius agnoscas: ut proximi mentem in tua invenias, et ex te noveris, qualiter illi subvenias, exemplo scilicet Salvatoris nostri, qui pati voluit, ut compati sciret; miser fieri, ut misereri disceret, ut quomodo de ipso scriptum est, Didicit ex his quae passus est obedientiam (Hebr. V, 8), ita et misericordiam disceret. Non quod ante misereri nesciret, cuius misericordia ab aeterno, et usque in aeternum: sed, quod natura sciebat ab aeterno, temporali didicit experimento.
english: I have said, as I could, with what fruit the steps of humility ought to be climbed: I will say, as I shall be able, in what order they lead to the appointed prize of truth. But because the knowledge of truth itself also consists in three steps, I distinguish them briefly, if I can, so that it may become clearer to which of the three of truth the twelfth of humility attains. For we seek the truth in ourselves, in our neighbors, and in its own nature. In ourselves, by judging ourselves; in our neighbors, by compassionating their evils; in its own nature, by contemplating with a pure heart. Observe the order as well as the number. First let Truth itself teach you that it ought to be sought in neighbors before it is sought in its own nature. After this you will learn why you ought to seek it in yourself before in your neighbors. For in the number of the Beatitudes, which the Lord distinguished in His sermon, He placed the merciful before the pure in heart (Matt. 5:7–8). The merciful quickly grasp the truth in their neighbors, while they stretch their affections toward them, and so conform themselves to them by charity that they feel their goods or their ills as their own. They are weak with the weak, they burn with those who are scandalized (2 Cor. 11:29). They have been accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). With the edge of the heart cleansed by this brotherly charity, they delight to contemplate the truth in its own nature, for love of which they bear the evils of others. But those who do not so associate themselves with their brothers, but on the contrary insult those who weep or belittle those who rejoice—while they do not feel in themselves what is in others, because they are not similarly affected—how can they grasp the truth in their neighbors? The common proverb fits them well: The healthy man does not know what the sick man feels, nor the full man what the hungry man suffers. And the sick man with the sick, and the hungry with the hungry, compassion the more familiarly as they are the nearer. For as pure truth is seen only by a pure heart, so a brother’s misery is more truly felt by a miserable heart. But that you may have a miserable heart because of another’s misery, you must first acknowledge your own, so that you may find your neighbor’s mind in your own, and may know from yourself how to help him: by the example, namely, of our Savior, who willed to suffer that He might know how to compassion, to become wretched that He might learn to have mercy, so that as it is written of Him, “He learned obedience from the things which He suffered” (Heb. 5:8), He might also learn mercy. Not that He who did not know how to have mercy beforehand—He whose mercy is from eternity and unto eternity—but that what He knew by nature from eternity, He learned by a temporal experiment.

chunks.latin: Non quod ante misereri nesciret, cuius misericordia ab aeterno, et usque in aeternum: sed, quod natura sciebat ab aeterno, temporali didicit experimento.
chunks.english: Not that He who did not know how to have mercy beforehand—He whose mercy is from eternity and unto eternity—but that what He knew by nature from eternity, He learned by a temporal experiment.

latin: Sed forte durum tibi videtur, quod dixi Dei sapientiam Christum didicisse misericordiam; quasi is per quem omnia facta sunt, aliquid aliquando ignorasset ex iis quae sunt: maxime cum illud quod ex Epistola ad Hebraeos ad id comprobandum commemoravi, alio sensu, qui non ita videatur absurdus, possit intelligi; ut hoc quod dictum est, didicit, non ad ipsum caput referatur in sui persona, sed ad corpus eius, quod est Ecclesia; et ita sit sensus: Et didicit ex iis quae passus est obedientiam, hoc est, obedientiam didicit in suo corpore ex iis quae passus est in capite. Nam illa mors, illa crux, opprobria, sputa, flagella, quae omnia caput nostrum Christus pertransiit, quid aliud corpori eius, id est nobis, quam praeclara obedientiae documenta fuerunt? Christus enim, ait Paulus, factus est obediens Patri usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis (Philipp. II, 8). Qua necessitate? Respondeat apostolus Petrus: Christus passus est pro nobis, vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini, inquit, vestigia eius (I Petr. II, 21), id est, ut imitemini obedientiam eius. Ex his ergo quae passus est, discimus quanta nos, qui puri homines sumus, oporteat pro obedientia perpeti, pro qua is, qui et Deus erat, non dubitaverit mori. Et hoc modo, inquis, non inconveniens erit, si dicatur Christus vel obedientiam, vel misericordiam, seu aliquid aliud in suo corpore didicisse: dum tamen sibi in sua persona nil, quod se ante latuerit, credatur ex tempore potuisse accedere. Sicque ipse sit qui misereri doceat aut obedire, ipse qui discat: quia caput et corpus unus est Christus.
english: But perhaps it seems hard to you that I have said that Christ, the Wisdom of God, learned mercy; as if He through whom all things were made had at some time been ignorant of something among the things that are: especially since that passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews which I recalled to prove this can be understood in another sense, which may not seem so absurd; so that this word “He learned” is referred not to the Head Himself in His own person, but to His body, which is the Church; and so the sense would be: “And He learned obedience from the things which He suffered,” that is, He learned obedience in His body from those things which He suffered in the Head. For that death, that cross, the insults, spittings, scourgings, all of which Christ our Head passed through—what else were they to His body, that is to us, than outstanding lessons of obedience? For “Christ,” says Paul, “became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2:8). By what necessity? Let the apostle Peter answer: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow,” he says, “His steps” (1 Pet. 2:21), that is, that you should imitate His obedience. From the things, then, which He suffered, we learn how much we, who are mere men, ought to endure for obedience, for which He who was also God did not hesitate to die. And in this way, you say, it will not be unfitting if Christ is said to have learned obedience, or mercy, or anything else in His body: provided only it is not believed that anything which had before been hidden from Him could have accrued to Him in His own person in time. And so He Himself would be the one who teaches how to have mercy or to obey, and Himself the one who learns: because Head and body are one Christ.

latin: Non nego hunc intellectum, quin rectus sit: sed ex alio loco ipsius Epistolae, superior interpretatio videtur approbari, ubi dicitur: Nusquam enim Angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahae apprehendit: unde debuit per omnia fratribus assimilari, ut misericors fieret (Hebr. II, 16, 17). Puto quod haec verba sic ad caput referenda sunt, ut corpori penitus aptari non possint. De Verbo utique Dei dictum est quod non Angelos apprehendit, hoc est, non in unam sibi personam assumpsit, sed semen Abrahae. Neque enim legitur, Verbum angelus factum est, sed Verbum caro factum est (Ioan. I, 14), et caro de carne Abrahae, iuxta promissionem, quae illi primum facta est. Unde, id est ex qua seminis assumptione, debuit per omnia fratribus assimilari; id est, oportuit ac necesse fuit, ut similis nobis passibilis, nostrarum omnia, excepto peccato, genera miseriarum percurreret. Si quaeris, qua necessitate? Ut misericors, inquit, fieret. Et hoc, ais, cur non recte ad corpus referri potest? Sed audi quod paulo post sequitur: In eo enim, in quo passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari (Hebr. II, 18). In quibus verbis quid melius intelligi possit non video; nisi quod ideo pati ac tentari, omnibusque, absque peccato, humanis voluit communicare miseriis (quod est per omnia fratribus simulari), ut similiter passis ac tentatis misereri ac compati ipse disceret experimento.
english: I do not deny that this understanding is a right one; but from another place in the same Epistle the former interpretation seems to be confirmed, where it is said: “For nowhere does He take hold of angels, but He takes hold of the seed of Abraham: whence He ought to be made like His brothers in all things, that He might become merciful” (Heb. 2:16–17). I think that these words are to be referred to the Head in such a way that they cannot at all be fitted to the body. It is said of the Word of God that He did not take hold of angels, that is, did not assume them into one person with Himself, but the seed of Abraham. For it is not read, “The Word was made an angel,” but “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), and flesh from the flesh of Abraham, according to the promise which was first made to him. Whence—that is, from this assumption of the seed—He ought to be made like His brothers in all things; that is, it was fitting and necessary that, passible like us, He should run through all the kinds of our miseries, except sin. If you ask, by what necessity? “That He might become merciful,” it says. And this, you say, why can it not rightly be referred to the body? But hear what follows a little later: “For in that in which He Himself has suffered and been tempted, He is able to help those also who are tempted” (Heb. 2:18). In which words I do not see what can better be understood, except that He therefore willed to suffer and to be tempted, and to share in all human miseries except sin (which is to be made like His brothers in all things), so that He Himself might learn by experience to have mercy and to compassion those similarly suffering and tempted.

latin: Quo quidem experimento non dico ut sapientior efficeretur, sed propinquior videretur: quatenus infirmi filii Adam, quos suos fieri et appellari fratres non dedignatus est (Ibid. 11), suas illi infirmitates committere non dubitarent, qui sanare illas et posset ut Deus, et vellet ut proximus, et cognosceret ut eadem passus. Unde Isaias virum eum appellat dolorum, et scientem infirmitatem (Isa. LIII, 3); et Apostolus: Non enim habemus, inquit, Pontificem qui non possit compati infirmitatibus nostris. Unde autem possit, indicans adiungit: Tentatum autem per omnia pro similitudine, absque peccato (Hebr. IV, 15). Beatus quippe Deus, beatus Dei Filius, in ea forma, qua non rapinam arbitratus est esse se aequalem Patri, procul dubio impassibilis, priusquam se exinanisset formam servi accipiens (Philipp. II, 6, 7), sicut miseriam vel subiectionem expertus non erat, sic misericordiam vel obedientiam non noverat experimento. Sciebat quidem per naturam, non autem sciebat per experientiam. At ubi minoratus est non solum a seipso, sed etiam paulo minus ab Angelis, qui et ipsi impassibiles sunt per gratiam, non per naturam, usque ad illam formam, in qua pati et subiici posset, quod utique (sicut dictum est) in sua non posset; et in passione expertus est misericordiam, et in subiectione obedientiam. Per quam tamen experientiam, non illi (ut dixi) scientia, sed nobis fiducia crevit, dum ex hoc misero genere cognitionis, is a quo longe erraveramus, factus est propior nobis. Quando enim illi appropinquare auderemus, in sua impassibilitate manenti? Nunc autem, Apostolo suadente, monemur cum fiducia adire thronum gratiae ipsius (Hebr. IV, 16), quem nimirum, sicut alibi scriptum est, languores nostros tulisse, et dolores nostros portasse cognoscimus (Isa. LIII, 4), et in eo quo passus est ipse, nobis compati posse non dubitamus.
english: By this experiment I do not say that He was made wiser, but that He was seen to be nearer: so that the weak sons of Adam, whom He did not disdain to make His own and to call His brothers (Heb. 2:11), might not hesitate to commit their infirmities to Him who could heal them as God, and would as a neighbor, and knew them as one who had suffered the same. Hence Isaiah calls Him a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity (Isa. 53:3); and the Apostle: “For we have not,” he says, “a High Priest who cannot compassion our infirmities.” And indicating whence He can, he adds: “but one tempted in all things after our likeness, without sin” (Heb. 4:15). For the blessed God, the blessed Son of God, in that form in which He did not think it robbery to be equal with the Father, was beyond doubt impassible, before He emptied Himself taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7); and as He had not experienced misery or subjection, so He had not known mercy or obedience by experiment. He knew them indeed by nature, but He did not know them by experience. But when He was made lower not only than Himself, but also a little lower than the angels, who themselves are impassible by grace, not by nature, down to that form in which He could suffer and be subjected, which (as has been said) He could not in His own; He experienced mercy in the Passion, and obedience in subjection. Yet by this experience, as I have said, it was not knowledge that grew in Him, but confidence in us, while by this wretched kind of knowing He from whom we had wandered far was made nearer to us. For when would we have dared to draw near to Him remaining in His impassibility? But now, as the Apostle urges, we are admonished to go with confidence to the throne of His grace (Heb. 4:16), whom surely, as it is written elsewhere, we know to have borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isa. 53:4), and we do not doubt that He can compassion us in that in which He Himself has suffered.

latin: Non ergo debet absurdum videri, si dicitur, Christum non quidem aliquid scire coepisse, quod aliquando nescierit; scire tamen alio modo misericordiam ab aeterno per divinitatem, et aliter in tempore didicisse per carnem. Vide ne et simili locutionis modo illud dictum sit, quod Dominus requirentibus discipulis de die ultimo se nescire respondit. Nam quomodo diem illum ille nesciebat, in quo omnes sapientiae et scientiae thesauri sunt absconditi? (Coloss. II, 3.) Cur ergo se scire negabat, quod certum est quia nescire non poterat? Numquid forte mendaciter eos voluit celare, quod utiliter non valuit innotescere? Absit. Sicut nil ignorare poterat, cum sapientia sit: sic nec mentiri, cum veritas sit. Sed volens discipulos ab inutilis inquisitionis curiositate compescere, quod inquirebant, se scire negavit: non omnino quidem, sed tali quodam modo, quo negare veraciter potuit. Nam, etsi suae divinitatis intuitu aeque omnia, praeterita scilicet, praesentia atque futura perlustrando, diem quoque illum palam habebat; non tamen ullis carnis suae sensibus experiendo agnoverat. Alioquin iam spiritu oris sui Antichristum interfecerat, iam auribus sui corporis archangelum vociferantem, et tubam sonantem, in quo strepitu mortui suscitandi sunt, audierat: iam oculis suae carnis oves haedosque, qui ab invicem segregandi sunt, perspexerat.
english: It ought not, then, to seem absurd if it is said that Christ did not indeed begin to know something which He had at some time not known, yet knew mercy in one way from eternity through the Godhead, and learned it in another way in time through the flesh. See whether that also was said in a similar manner of speaking, when the Lord, to the disciples asking about the last day, answered that He did not know it. For how did He not know that day, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden? (Col. 2:3.) Why then did He deny that He knew what it is certain He could not not know? Did He perhaps wish deceitfully to hide from them what He could not usefully make known? Far from it. As He could be ignorant of nothing, since He is Wisdom, so He could not lie, since He is Truth. But wishing to restrain the disciples from the curiosity of a useless inquiry, He denied that He knew what they were asking: not altogether, but in a certain manner in which He could truthfully deny it. For although by the gaze of His Godhead, surveying equally all things, past, present, and future, He also had that day openly; yet He had not come to know it by experiencing it with any senses of His flesh. Otherwise He would already have slain Antichrist with the spirit of His mouth; would already have heard with the ears of His body the archangel crying out and the trumpet sounding, at which noise the dead are to be raised; would already have seen with the eyes of His flesh the sheep and the goats who are to be separated from one another.

latin: Denique ut intelligas, quod illa tantum cognitione, quae per carnem fit, se illum diem nescire perhibuerit, vigilanter respondens, non ait: Nec ego scio, sed nec ipse, inquit, Filius hominis scit (Marc. XIII, 32). Quid est Filius hominis, nisi nomen assumptae carnis? Quo siquidem nomine intelligi datur, quia dicens se aliquid nescire, non iuxta quod Deus est, sed secundum hominem loquitur. Alias quippe loquens de se secundum suam divinitatem, non Filius, vel Filium hominis; Sed ego, vel Me, saepius ponere consuevit, ut ibi: Amen, amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum (Ioan. VIII, 58). Ego sum, ait: non, Filius hominis est. Nec dubium, quin de illa essentia diceret, qua ante Abraham et sine initio est, non qua post Abraham et ex Abraham factus est. Alibi quoque hominum de se opinionem a discipulis inquirens, Quem dicunt, inquit, homines esse, non me, sed Filium hominis? Rursus eosdem interrogans, qui de se ipsi quoque sentirent: Vos autem, non quem Filium hominis, sed quem me, ait, esse dicitis? Carnalis videlicet populi sententiam de carne inquirens, nomen carnis, quod proprie est Filius hominis, posuit: spirituales vero discipulos de sua divinitate interrogans, non Filium hominis, sed signanter me dixit. Quod denique Petrus intelligens, quid per hoc quod dixerat, me. requisiti fuissent, sua responsione aperuit: Tu es, inquiens, non Iesus filius Virginis, sed Christus Filius Dei (Matth. XVI, 13-16). Quod utique si respondisset, nihilominus veritatem dixisset: sed in verbis interrogationis sensum interrogantis prudenter advertens, competenter proprieque ad interrogata respondit, dicens: Tu es Christus, Filius Dei.
english: Finally, that you may understand that it was only by that knowledge which comes through the flesh that He declared Himself not to know that day, answering watchfully He does not say, “Nor do I know,” but “nor does the Son of Man Himself know” (Mark 13:32). What is “Son of Man,” if not the name of the assumed flesh? By which name it is given to be understood that, when He says He does not know something, He speaks not according to what He is as God, but according to man. For otherwise, speaking of Himself according to His divinity, He has more often been accustomed to put not “Son,” or “Son of Man,” but “I,” or “Me,” as there: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am” (John 8:58). “I am,” He says: not, “the Son of Man is.” And there is no doubt that He was speaking of that essence by which He is before Abraham and without beginning, not of that by which He was made after Abraham and from Abraham. Elsewhere also, inquiring of the disciples the opinion of men about Himself, “Whom,” He says, “do men say”—not Me, but—“the Son of Man is?” Again asking the same men what they themselves also thought of Him: “But you,” not “whom the Son of Man,” but “whom do you say that I am?” Inquiring, that is, the opinion of a carnal people about the flesh, He put the name of the flesh, which properly is Son of Man; but asking the spiritual disciples about His divinity, He said not “the Son of Man,” but pointedly “Me.” Which Peter at last understanding, showed by his answer what they had been asked by that “Me”: “You are,” he says, not “Jesus the son of the Virgin,” but “Christ the Son of God” (Matt. 16:13–16). Which if he had answered, he would nevertheless have said the truth; but prudently noticing in the words of the question the sense of the questioner, he answered the things asked fitly and properly, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of God.”

latin: Cum igitur videas Christum in una quidem persona duas habere naturas, unam qua semper fuit, alteram qua esse coepit; et secundum sempiternum suum quidem esse, semper omnia nosse; secundum temporalem vero, multa temporaliter expertum fuisse: cur fateri dubitas, ut esse in tempore coepit ex carne, sic carnis quoque miserias scire coepisse, illo duntaxat modo cognitionis, quem docet defectio carnis? Quod utique genus scientiae protoplasti sapientius feliciusque nescirent, quando id attingere nisi stulte misereque non poterant. Sed plasmator eorum Deus requirens quod perierat, opus suum miseratus prosecutus est, descendens et ipse misericorditer, quo illi ceciderant miserabiliter. Voluit experiri in se, quod illi faciendo contra se merito paterentur, non simili quidem curiositate, sed mirabili caritate: non ut miser cum miseris remaneret, sed ut misericors factus miseros liberaret. Factus, inquam, misericors, non illa misericordia, quam felix manens habuit ab aeterno, sed quam mediante miseria reperit in habitu nostro. Porro pietatis opus, quod per illam coepit, in ista perfecit: non quod sola illa non posset perficere; sed quia nobis non potuit absque ista sufficere. Utraque siquidem necessaria; sed nobis haec magis congrua fuit. O ineffabilis pietatis excogitatio! Quando nos illam miram misericordiam cogitaremus, quam praecedens miseria non informat? Quando illam adverteremus incognitam nobis compassionem, quae non passione praeventa, cum impassibilitate perdurat? Attamen si illa, quae miseriam nescit misericordia non praecessisset, ad hanc, cuius miseria mater est, non accessisset. Si non accessisset, non attraxisset: si non attraxisset, non extraxisset. Unde autem extraxit, nisi de lacu miseriae, et de luto faecis? (Psal. XXXIX, 3.) Nec illam tamen misericordiam deseruit, sed hanc inseruit: non mutavit, sed multiplicavit, sicut scriptum est: Homines et iumenta salvabis, Domine, quemadmodum multiplicasti misericordiam tuam, Deus (Psal. XXXV, 7, 8).
english: Since therefore you see that Christ has two natures in one person, one by which He always was, the other by which He began to be; and according to His eternal being always knew all things, but according to the temporal was experienced in many things in time: why do you hesitate to confess that, as He began to be in time from the flesh, so He also began to know the miseries of the flesh, at least by that mode of knowing which the weakness of the flesh teaches? Which kind of knowledge our first parents would more wisely and more happily have not known, since they could not attain it except foolishly and miserably. But God their Fashioner, seeking what had perished, in mercy followed His own work, Himself descending mercifully to where they had fallen miserably. He willed to experience in Himself what they deservedly suffered by acting against Him, not indeed with a like curiosity, but with marvelous charity: not that He might remain wretched with the wretched, but that, having become merciful, He might free the wretched. Having become, I say, merciful, not with that mercy which, remaining blessed, He had from eternity, but with that which, by the medium of misery, He found in our habit. Further, the work of piety which He began by the former He completed in the latter: not because the former alone could not complete it, but because for us it could not suffice without this latter. Both were necessary; but this was more fitting for us. O unspeakable device of piety! When would we have thought of that wondrous mercy which preceding misery does not shape? When would we have noticed that compassion unknown to us which, not preceded by passion, endures with impassibility? Yet if that mercy which knows no misery had not gone before, He would not have come to this whose mother is misery. If He had not come, He would not have drawn; if He had not drawn, He would not have drawn out. And from where did He draw out, if not from the pit of misery and the mire of dregs? (Ps. 39:3.) Yet He did not abandon that former mercy, but inserted this; He did not change it, but multiplied it, as it is written: “Men and beasts You will save, O Lord: how You have multiplied Your mercy, O God” (Ps. 35:7–8).

heading: CAPUT IV. Primus veritatis gradus est, primum seipsum attendere, seu propriam miseriam agnoscere
latin: CAPUT IV. Primus veritatis gradus est, primum seipsum attendere, seu propriam miseriam agnoscere.
english: Chapter IV. The first step of truth is first to attend to oneself, or to acknowledge one’s own misery.
label: CAPUT IV. Primus veritatis gradus est, primum seipsum attendere, seu propriam miseriam agnoscere

chunks.latin: CAPUT IV. Primus veritatis gradus est, primum seipsum attendere, seu propriam miseriam agnoscere.
chunks.english: Chapter IV. The first step of truth is first to attend to oneself, or to acknowledge one’s own misery.

latin: Sed iam ad propositum redeamus. Si ergo se miserum fecit, qui miser non erat, ut experiretur quod et ante sciebat: quanto magis tu, non dico ut te facias quod non es, sed ut attendas quod es, quia vere miser es, et sic discas misereri, qui hoc aliter scire non potes! ne forte, si proximi malum consideres, et tuum non attendas, movearis non ad miserationem, sed ad indignationem; non ad adiuvandum, sed ad iudicandum: denique non ad instruendum in spiritu lenitatis, sed ad destruendum in spiritu furoris. Vos, qui spirituales estis, ait Apostolus, huiusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis. Apostoli consilium sive etiam praeceptum est, ut mansueto, id est eo spiritu fratri aegrotanti subvenias, quo tibi vis subveniri cum aegrotas. Et ut scias qualiter erga delinquentem mansuescere possis, Considerans, inquit, teipsum, ne et tu tenteris (Galat. VI, 1).
english: But let us now return to our purpose. If then He who was not wretched made Himself wretched, that He might experience what He also knew before: how much more should you—I do not say make yourself what you are not, but attend to what you are, because you are truly wretched, and so learn to have mercy, who cannot otherwise know this! Lest perhaps, if you consider your neighbor’s evil and do not attend to your own, you be moved not to pity but to indignation; not to helping, but to judging; finally not to instructing in the spirit of meekness, but to destroying in the spirit of fury. “You who are spiritual,” says the Apostle, “instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness.” It is the Apostle’s counsel, or even command, that you should succor a sick brother with that meek spirit with which you wish to be succored when you are sick. And that you may know how you can grow meek toward one who goes astray, “considering yourself,” he says, “lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

latin: Considerare libet, quam bene discipulus Veritatis ordinem sequatur Magistri. In beatitudinibus, quas supra memoravi (num. 6), sicut prius misericordes quam mundicordes, sic prius mites quam misericordes pronuntiati sunt (Matth. V, 4, 7, 8). Et Apostolus cum spirituales hortaretur ad instruendum carnales, adiunxit, in spiritu lenitatis. Instructio quippe fratrum pertinet ad misericordes; spiritus lenitatis, ad mites. Ac si diceret: Inter misericordes deputari non potest, qui in semetipso mitis non est. Ecce Apostolus aperte ostendit, quod superius me ostensurum promisi (num. 6), prius videlicet veritatem inquirendam esse in nobis, quam in proximis; considerans, inquiens, teipsum, id est, quam facilis ad tentandum, quam pronus ad peccandum: quatenus ex tui consideratione mitescas, sicque ad succurrendum aliis in spiritu lenitatis accedas. Alioquin si monentem non audis discipulum, arguentem time Magistrum: Hypocrita, eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo; et sic videbis festucam eiicere de oculo fratris tui(Matth. VII, 5). Trabes in oculo grandis et grossa, superbia in mente est: quae quadam corpulentia sui vana, non sana; tumida, non solida, oculum mentis obscurat, veritatem obumbrat: ita ut, si tuam occupaverit mentem, iam tu te videre, iam te talem, qualis es, vel qualis esse potes, non possis sentire: sed qualem te amas, talem te vel putes esse, vel speres fore. Quid enim aliud est superbia, quam (ut quidam sanctus definit), amor propriae excellentiae? Unde et nos possumus dicere per contrarium, humilitatem propriae et excellentiae esse contemptum. Amor vero, sicut nec odium, veritatis iudicium nescit. Vis iudicium Veritatis audire! Sicut audio, sic iudico(Ioan. V, 30). Non sicut odi, non sicut amo, non sicut timeo. Est iudicium odii, ut illud: Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem nostram debet mori(Ioan. XIX, 7). Est et timoris, ut illud: Si dimittimus eum sic, venient Romani et tollent nostrum locum et gentem (Ioan. XI, 48). Iudicium vero amoris, ut David de filio parricida: Parcite, inquit, puero Absalon(II Reg. XVIII, 5). Et legibus humanis statutum, et in causis, tam ecclesiasticis, quam saecularibus servatum scio, speciales amicos causantium non debere admitti ad iudicium: ne vel fallant, vel fallantur amore suorum. Quod si culpam amici tuo iudicio amor illius aut minuit, aut prorsus abscondit: quanto magis amor tui tuum contra te iudicium fallit!
english: It is worth considering how well the disciple of Truth follows the order of the Master. In the Beatitudes, which I recalled above (n. 6), as the merciful were named before the pure in heart, so the meek before the merciful (Matt. 5:4, 7, 8). And the Apostle, when he exhorted the spiritual to instruct the carnal, added, “in the spirit of meekness.” For the instruction of the brothers belongs to the merciful; the spirit of meekness, to the meek. As if he said: He cannot be reckoned among the merciful who is not meek in himself. See, the Apostle openly shows what I promised above I would show (n. 6), namely that the truth is first to be sought in us rather than in our neighbors; “considering,” he says, “yourself,” that is, how easy to temptation, how prone to sin: so that from the consideration of yourself you may grow meek, and so come to help others in the spirit of meekness. Otherwise, if you do not hear the disciple warning, fear the Master accusing: “Hypocrite, cast out first the beam from your own eye; and then you will see to cast out the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:5). The beam in the eye, great and thick, is pride in the mind: which by a certain bulk of itself, vain not sound, swollen not solid, darkens the eye of the mind and overshadows the truth: so that if it has occupied your mind, you can no longer see yourself, no longer feel yourself such as you are, or such as you can be; but such as you love, such you either think yourself to be, or hope to become. For what else is pride than (as a certain saint defines it) the love of one’s own excellence? Whence we also can say by contrary, that humility is the contempt of one’s own excellence. But love, as hatred also, does not know the judgment of truth. Do you wish to hear the judgment of Truth? “As I hear, so I judge” (John 5:30). Not as I hate, not as I love, not as I fear. There is a judgment of hatred, as that: “We have a law, and according to our law He ought to die” (John 19:7). There is also one of fear, as that: “If we let Him so, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). But a judgment of love, as David concerning his parricide son: “Spare,” he says, “the boy Absalom” (2 Sam. 18:5). And I know it is laid down by human laws, and observed in causes both ecclesiastical and secular, that the special friends of the litigants ought not to be admitted to judgment: lest they either deceive or be deceived by love of their own. And if the love of a friend either lessens his fault in your judgment, or wholly hides it: how much more does love of yourself deceive your judgment against yourself!

Otherwise, if you do not hear the disciple warning, fear the Master accusing: “Hypocrite, cast out first the beam from your own eye; and then you will see to cast out the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:5).

chunks.latin: Trabes in oculo grandis et grossa, superbia in mente est: quae quadam corpulentia sui vana, non sana; tumida, non solida, oculum mentis obscurat, veritatem obumbrat: ita ut, si tuam occupaverit mentem, iam tu te videre, iam te talem, qualis es, vel qualis esse potes, non possis sentire: sed qualem te amas, talem te vel putes esse, vel speres fore.
chunks.english: The beam in the eye, great and thick, is pride in the mind: which by a certain bulk of itself, vain not sound, swollen not solid, darkens the eye of the mind and overshadows the truth: so that if it has occupied your mind, you can no longer see yourself, no longer feel yourself such as you are, or such as you can be; but such as you love, such you either think yourself to be, or hope to become.

chunks.latin: Quid enim aliud est superbia, quam (ut quidam sanctus definit), amor propriae excellentiae? Unde et nos possumus dicere per contrarium, humilitatem propriae et excellentiae esse contemptum. Amor vero, sicut nec odium, veritatis iudicium nescit. Vis iudicium Veritatis audire! Sicut audio, sic iudico(Ioan. V, 30). Non sicut odi, non sicut amo, non sicut timeo.
chunks.english: For what else is pride than (as a certain saint defines it) the love of one’s own excellence? Whence we also can say by contrary, that humility is the contempt of one’s own excellence.

chunks.latin: Est iudicium odii, ut illud: Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem nostram debet mori(Ioan. XIX, 7). Est et timoris, ut illud: Si dimittimus eum sic, venient Romani et tollent nostrum locum et gentem (Ioan. XI, 48).
chunks.english: But love, as hatred also, does not know the judgment of truth. Do you wish to hear the judgment of Truth? “As I hear, so I judge” (John 5:30). Not as I hate, not as I love, not as I fear. There is a judgment of hatred, as that: “We have a law, and according to our law He ought to die” (John 19:7). There is also one of fear, as that: “If we let Him so, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48).

chunks.latin: Iudicium vero amoris, ut David de filio parricida: Parcite, inquit, puero Absalon(II Reg. XVIII, 5). Et legibus humanis statutum, et in causis, tam ecclesiasticis, quam saecularibus servatum scio, speciales amicos causantium non debere admitti ad iudicium: ne vel fallant, vel fallantur amore suorum. Quod si culpam amici tuo iudicio amor illius aut minuit, aut prorsus abscondit: quanto magis amor tui tuum contra te iudicium fallit!
chunks.english: But a judgment of love, as David concerning his parricide son: “Spare,” he says, “the boy Absalom” (2 Sam. 18:5). And I know it is laid down by human laws, and observed in causes both ecclesiastical and secular, that the special friends of the litigants ought not to be admitted to judgment: lest they either deceive or be deceived by love of their own. And if the love of a friend either lessens his fault in your judgment, or wholly hides it: how much more does love of yourself deceive your judgment against yourself!

latin: Qui ergo plene veritatem in se cognoscere curat, necesse est ut semota trabe superbiae, quae oculum arcet a luce, ascensiones in corde suo disponat, per quas seipsum in seipso inquirat, et sic post duodecimum humilitatis ad primum veritatis gradum pertingat. Cum autem veritate inventa in se, imo se invento in veritate, dicere potuerit, Credidi, propter quod locutus sum; ego autem humiliatus sum nimis: ascendat homo ad cor altum, ut exaltetur veritas, et ad gradum secundum perveniens dicat in excessu suo: Omnis homo mendax (Psal. CXV, 10, 11). Putas, hunc ordinem David non tenuit! Putas, hoc non sensit Propheta, quod Dominus, quod Apostolus, quod et nos post ipsos, et per ipsos sentimus! Credidi, inquit, Veritati dicenti: Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris (Ioan. VIII, 12). Credidi ergo sequendo, propter quod locutus sum confitendo. Quid confitendo! Veritatem quam cognovi credendo. Postquam autem et credidi ad iustitiam, et locutus sum ad salutem, humiliatus sum nimis, hoc est perfecte. Tanquam diceret: Quia veritatem cognitam in me confiteri contra me non erubui, ad perfectionem humilitatis profeci. Nimis enim pro Perfecte potest intelligi; ut ibi: In mandatis eius volet nimis (Psal. CXI, 1). Quod si quis contendat, nimis hic pro Valde positum non pro Perfecte, quia et expositores id ipsum videntur astruere; neque hoc discordat a sensu Prophetae, ut sic sentiamus eum dixisse: Ego quidem, cum adhuc veritatem non nossem, aliquid me putabam esse, cum nihil essem. At postquam in Christum credendo, id est eius humilitatem imitando, veritatem agnovi; ipsa quidem exaltata est in me ex mea confessione: sed ego humiliatus sum nimis, id est, valde vilui mihi ex mei consideratione.
english: Whoever therefore cares to know the truth fully in himself must, when the beam of pride which keeps the eye from the light has been removed, set ascents in his heart, by which he may seek himself in himself, and so after the twelfth of humility reach the first step of truth. And when, the truth having been found in himself—or rather himself found in the truth—he can say, “I believed, therefore I have spoken; but I was humbled exceedingly”: let a man ascend to a high heart, that the truth may be exalted, and coming to the second step say in his excess: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. 115:10–11). Do you think David did not keep this order? Do you think the Prophet did not feel this, which the Lord, which the Apostle, which we also after them and through them feel? “I believed,” he says, the Truth saying: “He who follows Me does not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). I believed therefore by following, “therefore I have spoken” by confessing. What by confessing? The truth which I came to know by believing. But after I both believed unto justice and spoke unto salvation, “I was humbled exceedingly,” that is, perfectly. For “exceedingly” can be understood as “perfectly”; as there: “He will delight exceedingly in His commandments” (Ps. 111:1). But if anyone contends that “exceedingly” is put here for “greatly,” not for “perfectly,” because the expositors also seem to maintain this: even this does not discord from the Prophet’s sense, so that we may take him to have said: I indeed, while I did not yet know the truth, thought myself to be something, when I was nothing. But after, by believing in Christ, that is by imitating His humility, I came to know the truth, it was indeed exalted in me by my confession: but I was humbled exceedingly, that is, I became very cheap to myself from the consideration of myself.

heading: CAPUT V. Secundus gradus veritatis est, ex agnitione propriae infirmitatis, compati miseriae proximi
latin: CAPUT V. Secundus gradus veritatis est, ex agnitione propriae infirmitatis, compati miseriae proximi.
english: Chapter V. The second step of truth is, from the knowledge of one’s own infirmity, to compassion the misery of one’s neighbor.
label: CAPUT V. Secundus gradus veritatis est, ex agnitione propriae infirmitatis, compati miseriae proximi

chunks.latin: CAPUT V. Secundus gradus veritatis est, ex agnitione propriae infirmitatis, compati miseriae proximi.
chunks.english: Chapter V. The second step of truth is, from the knowledge of one’s own infirmity, to compassion the misery of one’s neighbor.

latin: Humiliatus ergo Propheta in hoc primo gradu veritatis, ut ait in alio psalmo: Et in veritate tua humiliasti me (Psal. CXVIII, 75); semetipsum attendat, et ex propria miseria generalem perpendat: sicque ad secundum transiens dicat in excessu suo, Omnis homo mendax. In quo excessu suo? In illo procul dubio, quo sese excedens, ac veritati adhaerens, seipsum diiudicat. In illo ergo excessu suo dicat, non indignando aut insultando, sed miserando et compatiendo: Omnis homo mendax. Quid est, Omnis homo mendax? Omnis homo infirmus, omnis homo miser et impotens, qui nec se, nec alium possit salvare. Sicut dicitur: Fallax equus ad salutem (Psal. XXXII, 17), non quod equus aliquem fallat, sed quia is seipsum fallit, qui in fortitudine eius confidit: sic omnis homo dicitur mendax, id est fragilis, mutabilis, a quo salus non possit vel sua, vel aliena sperari: quin potius maledictionem incurrat, qui spem suam in homine ponit (Ierem. XVII, 5). Proficiens itaque humilis Propheta per ducatum veritatis, quodque in se lugebat videns in aliis, dum apponit scientiam, apponat et dolorem, ac generaliter, sed veraciter dicat: Omnis homo mendax.
english: The Prophet, then, humbled in this first step of truth, as he says in another psalm: “And in Your truth You have humbled me” (Ps. 118:75), let him attend to himself, and from his own misery weigh the general; and so passing to the second let him say in his excess, “Every man is a liar.” In what excess of his? In that, surely, in which, exceeding himself and clinging to the truth, he judges himself. In that excess of his, then, let him say, not with indignation or insult, but with pity and compassion: “Every man is a liar.” What is “Every man is a liar”? Every man is weak, every man wretched and powerless, who can save neither himself nor another. As it is said: “A horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. 32:17), not that the horse deceives anyone, but because he deceives himself who trusts in its strength: so every man is called a liar, that is fragile, changeable, from whom neither his own salvation nor another’s can be hoped: rather he incurs a curse who puts his hope in man (Jer. 17:5). The humble Prophet, then, advancing under the guidance of truth, and seeing in others what he lamented in himself, while he adds knowledge, let him also add grief, and generally but truly say: “Every man is a liar.”

latin: Vide quam longe aliud senserit de se Pharisaeus ille superbus. Quid deprompsit in excessu suo? Deus, gratias ago tibi, quia non sum sicut caeteri hominum (Luc. XVIII, 11). Dum in se singulariter exsultat, aliis arroganter insultat. David autem aliter. Ait enim: Omnis homo mendax. Neminem excipit, ne quem decipiat: sciens quia omnes peccaverunt, et omnes egent gloria Dei (Rom. III, 23). Pharisaeus se solum decipit, quem solum excipit, dum caeteros damnat. Propheta se non excipit a communi miseria, ne excipiatur a misericordia: Pharisaeus exsufflat misericordiam, dum dissimulat miseriam. Propheta affirmat tam de omnibus, quam de se: Omnis homo mendax: Pharisaeus confirmat de omnibus praeter se, Non sum, inquiens, sicut caeteri hominum Et gratias agit, non quia bonus, sed quia solus: non tam de bonis quae habet, quam de malis quae in aliis videt. Nondum de suo trabem eiecerat, et festucas in oculis fratrum enumerat. Nam subdit: Iniusti, captores (Luc. XVIII, 11). Non frustra, ut arbitror, excessum a proposito feci, si utriusque excessus differentiam intellexisti.
english: See how far otherwise that proud Pharisee felt about himself. What did he bring out in his excess? “God, I thank You that I am not as the rest of men” (Luke 18:11). While he exults in himself singularly, he arrogantly insults others. But David speaks otherwise. For he says: “Every man is a liar.” He excepts no one, lest he deceive anyone: knowing that all have sinned, and all lack the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). The Pharisee deceives himself alone, whom alone he excepts, while he condemns the rest. The Prophet does not except himself from the common misery, lest he be excepted from mercy: the Pharisee blows away mercy, while he disguises misery. The Prophet affirms as of all, so of himself: “Every man is a liar”: the Pharisee confirms it of all except himself, “I am not,” he says, “as the rest of men.” And he gives thanks, not because he is good, but because he is alone: not so much for the goods he has, as for the evils he sees in others. He had not yet cast the beam out of his own, and he counts the specks in his brothers’ eyes. For he adds: “unjust, extortioners” (Luke 18:11). Not in vain, I think, have I gone aside from the purpose, if you have understood the difference of both excesses.

Nondum de suo trabem eiecerat, et festucas in oculis fratrum enumerat. Nam subdit: Iniusti, captores (Luc. XVIII, 11). Non frustra, ut arbitror, excessum a proposito feci, si utriusque excessus differentiam intellexisti.

latin: Iam ad propositum redeundum est. Quos itaque veritas sibi iam innotescere, ac per hoc vilescere fecit, necesse est, ut cuncta, quae amare solebant, et ipsi sibi amarescant. Statuentes nimirum se ante se, tales se videre cogunt, quales vel a se videri erubescunt. Dumque sibi displicet quod sunt, et ad id suspirant quod non sunt, quod utique per se fore diffidunt; vehementer sese lugentes id solum consolationis inveniunt, ut severi iudices sui, qui scilicet amore veri esuriant et sitiant iustitiam, usque ad contemptum sui districtissimam de se exigant satisfactionem, et de caetero emendationem. Sed, cum se ad id sufficere non posse conspiciunt (cum enim fecerint omnia quae mandata fuerint sibi, servos se inutiles dicunt (Luc. XVII, 10), de iustitia ad misericordiam confugiunt. Ut autem illam consequantur, consilium Veritatis sequuntur: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur (Matth. V, 7). Et hic est secundus gradus veritatis, quo eam in proximis inquirunt; dum de suis aliorum necessitates exquirunt; dum ex iis quae patiuntur, patientibus compati sciunt.
english: Now we must return to the purpose. Those, then, whom the truth has already made known to themselves, and thereby made cheap, it is necessary that all the things they were accustomed to love, and they themselves to themselves, should grow bitter. Setting themselves before themselves, they compel themselves to see themselves such as they blush to be seen even by themselves. And while what they are displeases them, and they sigh for what they are not, which they wholly distrust they can be by themselves; weeping over themselves vehemently, they find this only consolation, that as severe judges of themselves, who for love of the true hunger and thirst for justice, they exact from themselves a most strict satisfaction even to self-contempt, and amendment for the future. But when they see that they cannot suffice for this (for when they have done all that was commanded them, they say they are unprofitable servants (Luke 17:10)), they flee from justice to mercy. And that they may obtain it, they follow the counsel of Truth: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). And this is the second step of truth, by which they seek it in their neighbors; while from their own they search out the needs of others; while from the things they suffer they know how to compassion those who suffer.

latin: CAPUT VI. Tertius gradus veritatis, mundare oculum cordis ad contemplanda coelestia et divina.
english: Chapter VI. The third step of truth: to cleanse the eye of the heart for contemplating heavenly and divine things.

chunks.latin: CAPUT VI. Tertius gradus veritatis, mundare oculum cordis ad contemplanda coelestia et divina.
chunks.english: Chapter VI. The third step of truth: to cleanse the eye of the heart for contemplating heavenly and divine things.

latin: In his ergo tribus quae dicta sunt, id est in luctu poenitentiae, in desiderio iustitiae, in operibus misericordiae si perseverant, a tribus impedimentis, quae aut ignorantia, aut infirmitate, aut studio contraxerunt, cordis aciem mundant, quo per contemplationem ad tertium veritatis gradum pertranseant. Hae sunt viae, quae videntur hominibus bonae, illis duntaxat exceptis, qui laetantur cum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis (Prov. II, 14), ac se de infirmitate vel ignorantia tegunt ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis (Psal. CXL, 4). Sed frustra sibi de infirmitate, vel ignorantia blandiuntur, qui ut liberius peccent, libenter ignorant, vel infirmantur. Putas, primo homini profuit, licet ipse non libenter peccavit, quod se per uxorem, tanquam per carnis infirmitatem, defendit (Gen. III, 12)? aut primi martyris lapidatores, quoniam aures suas continuerunt (Act. VII, 56), per ignorantiam excusabiles erunt? Qui igitur studio et amore peccandi a veritate se sentiunt alienatos, infirmitate et ignorantia pressos; studium in gemitum, amorem in moerorem convertant, infirmitatem carnis fervore iustitiae vincant, ignorantiam liberalitate repellant: ne si nunc egentem, nudam et infirmam veritatem ignorant, cum potestate magna et virtute venientem, terrentem, arguentem, sero cum rubore cognoscant, frustra cum tremore respondeant: Quando te vidimus egere, et non ministravimus tibi? (Matth. XXV, 44.) Cognoscetur certe Dominus iudicia faciens (Psal. IX, 17), qui nunc ignoratur misericordiam quaerens. Denique videbunt in quem transfixerunt (Ioan. XIX, 37): similiter et avari quem contempserunt. Ab omni ergo labe, infirmitate, ignorantia studiove contracta, flendo, iustitiam esuriendo, operibus misericordiae insistendo, mundatur oculus cordis, cui se in sui puritate Veritas videndam promittit: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (Matth. V, 8). Cum sint itaque tres gradus seu status veritatis, ad primum ascendimus per laborem humilitatis, ad secundum per affectum compassionis, ad tertium per excessum contemplationis. In primo veritas reperitur severa; in secundo, pia; in tertio, pura. Ad primum ratio ducit, qua nos discutimus; ad secundum affectus perducit, quo aliis miseremur; ad tertium puritas rapit, qua ad invisibilia sublevamur.
english: If then they persevere in these three things that have been said, that is in the mourning of penitence, in the desire of justice, in the works of mercy, they cleanse the edge of the heart from the three hindrances which they contracted either by ignorance, or by infirmity, or by zeal, so that through contemplation they may pass over to the third step of truth. These are ways that seem good to men, those only excepted who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2:14), and cover themselves with infirmity or ignorance to make excuses in sins (Ps. 140:4). But in vain do they flatter themselves with infirmity or ignorance, who, that they may sin more freely, willingly are ignorant or infirm. Do you think it profited the first man, even though he did not sin willingly, that he defended himself through his wife, as through the infirmity of the flesh (Gen. 3:12)? Or will the stoners of the first martyr, because they stopped their ears (Acts 7:56), be excusable through ignorance? Those therefore who feel themselves alienated from the truth by the zeal and love of sinning, pressed by infirmity and ignorance, let them turn zeal into groaning, love into mourning, let them conquer the infirmity of the flesh by the fervor of justice, let them drive out ignorance by generosity: lest if they now ignore the needy, naked, and infirm truth, they come to know her too late, with shame, when she comes with great power and virtue, terrifying and accusing, and answer in vain with trembling: “When did we see You in need, and did not minister to You?” (Matt. 25:44.) The Lord will surely be known when He executes judgments (Ps. 9:17), who is now ignored when He seeks mercy. Finally they shall look on Him whom they pierced (John 19:37): and likewise the avaricious on Him whom they despised. From every stain, then, contracted by infirmity, ignorance, or zeal, by weeping, by hungering for justice, by clinging to works of mercy, the eye of the heart is cleansed, to which Truth promises herself to be seen in her own purity: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Since there are three steps or states of truth, we climb to the first by the labor of humility, to the second by the affection of compassion, to the third by the excess of contemplation. In the first, truth is found severe; in the second, kind; in the third, pure. To the first, reason leads, by which we examine ourselves; to the second, affection brings us, by which we pity others; to the third, purity snatches us, by which we are lifted to invisible things.
