heading: CAPUT VII. Quomodo sancta Trinitas hos tres veritatis gradus in nobis operetur
latin: CAPUT VII. Quomodo sancta Trinitas hos tres veritatis gradus in nobis operetur.
english: Chapter VII. How the Holy Trinity works these three steps of truth in us.
label: CAPUT VII. Quomodo sancta Trinitas hos tres veritatis gradus in nobis operetur

chunks.latin: CAPUT VII. Quomodo sancta Trinitas hos tres veritatis gradus in nobis operetur.
chunks.english: Chapter VII. How the Holy Trinity works these three steps of truth in us.

latin: Interlucet hic mihi mira quaedam ac divisa individuae Trinitatis operatio, si quo modo tamen ab homine sedente in tenebris ineffabilis illa possit capi cooperantium sibi personarum divisio. In primo siquidem gradu Filius, in secundo Spiritus sanctus, in tertio mihi Pater operari videtur. Vis audire Filii operationem? Si ego, inquit, lavi vobis pedes Dominus et magister, quanto magis et vos debetis alter alterius lavare pedes? (Ioan. XIII, 14.) Tradebat discipulis humilitatis formam veritatis Magister, qua in primo gradu primum eis veritas innotesceret. Attende et opus Spiritus sancti: Caritas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis (Rom. V, 5). Caritas quippe donum est Spiritus sancti, qua fit ut qui sub disciplina Filii per humilitatem ad primum usque gradum veritatis iam profecerunt, ad secundum per compassionem proximi, sub magisterio Spiritus sancti perveniant. Audi et de Patre, Beatus es, Simon Bar Iona, quia caro et sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed Pater meus qui est in coelis (Matth. XVI, 17); et illud, Pater filiis notam faciet veritatem suam (Isai. XXXVIII, 19); et, Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus, et revelasti ea parvulis (Matth. XI, 25): Vides quia quos verbo et exemplo prius Filius humiliavit, super quos deinde Spiritus sanctus caritatem effudit, hos tandem in gloria Pater recepit? Filius facit discipulos, Paraclitus consolatur amicos, Pater exaltat filios. Quia vero non solum Filius, sed et Pater et Spiritus sanctus veraciter Veritas appellantur; constat quod una eademque Veritas, servata proprietate personarum, tria haec in tribus gradibus operatur. Primo scilicet instruit, ut magister: secundo consolatur, ut amicus vel frater: tertio astringit, ut filios pater.
english: Here a certain wondrous and distributed operation of the undivided Trinity shines through to me, if somehow that ineffable distinction of the persons cooperating with one another can be grasped by a man sitting in darkness. In the first step the Son, in the second the Holy Spirit, in the third the Father seems to me to work. Do you wish to hear the operation of the Son? “If I,” He says, “the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, how much more ought you also to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:14.) The Master of truth was handing to the disciples the form of humility, by which in the first step the truth might first become known to them. Attend also to the work of the Holy Spirit: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). For charity is the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which it comes about that those who under the discipline of the Son have already advanced through humility as far as the first step of truth, come to the second through compassion of the neighbor, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Hear also of the Father: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but My Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17); and this: “The Father will make His truth known to the children” (Isa. 38:19); and, “I confess to You, Father, because You have hidden these things from the wise, and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). Do you see that those whom the Son first humbled by word and example, upon whom the Holy Spirit then poured charity, the Father at last received in glory? The Son makes disciples, the Paraclete consoles friends, the Father exalts sons. And because not only the Son, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit are truly called Truth, it is clear that one and the same Truth, the property of the persons being kept, works these three things in the three steps. First, namely, He instructs, as a master; second, He consoles, as a friend or brother; third, He binds, as a father His sons.

latin: Dei quippe Filius, Verbum scilicet ac sapientia Patris, primum quidem illam animae nostrae potentiam, quae ratio dicitur, cum reperit carne depressam, peccato captivam, ignorantia caecam, exterioribus deditam; clementer assumens, potenter erigens, prudenter instruens, introrsum trahens, ac mirabiliter utens tanquam pro se vicaria, ipsam sibi iudicem statuit, ita ut pro reverentia Verbi cui coniungitur, ipsa sui accusatrix, testis, et iudex, contra se Veritatis fungatur officio. Ex qua prima coniunctione Verbi et rationis humilitas nascitur. Aliam deinde partem, quae dicitur voluntas, veneno quidem carnis infectam, sed iam ratione discussam, Spiritus sanctus dignanter visitans, suaviter pugnans, ardenter afficiens, misericordem facit: ita ut more pellis, quae uncta extenditur, ipsa quoque unctione perfusa coelesti usque ad inimicos per affectum dilatetur. Et sic ex hac secunda coniunctione Spiritus Dei et voluntatis humanae, caritas efficitur. Utramque vero partem, rationem scilicet et voluntatem, alteram verbo veritatis instructam, alteram spiritu veritatis afflatam; illam hyssopo humilitatis aspersam, hanc igne caritatis succensam; tandem iam perfectam animam, propter humilitatem sine macula, propter caritatem sine ruga; cum nec voluntas rationi repugnat, nec ratio veritatem dissimulat, gloriosam sibi sponsam Pater conglutinat: ita ut nec ratio de se, nec voluntas de proximo cogitare sinatur, sed hoc solum beata illa anima dicere delectetur, Introduxit me Rex in cubiculum suum. Digna certe, quae de schola humilitatis, in qua primum sub magistro Filio ad seipsam intrare didicit, iuxta comminationem ad se factam, Si ignoras te, egredere et pasce haedos tuos (Cantic. I, 3, 7); digna ergo, quae de schola illa humilitatis duce Spiritu sancto in cellaria caritatis (quae nimirum proximorum pectora intelligenda sunt) per affectionem introduceretur; unde suffulta floribus, ac stipata malis, bonis scilicet moribus et virtutibus sanctis, ad Regis demum cubiculum, cuius amore languet, admitteretur. Ibi modicum, hora videlicet quasi dimidia, silentio facto in coelo, inter desideratos amplexus suaviter quiescens, ipsa quidem dormit, sed cor eius vigilat, quo utique interim veritatis arcana rimatur: quorum postmodum memoria statim ad se reditura pascatur. Ibi videt invisibilia, audit ineffabilia, quae non licet homini loqui. Excedunt quippe omnem illam, quam nox nocti indicat, scientiam: dies tamen diei eructat verbum, et inter sapientes sapientiam loqui et spiritualibus spiritualia licet conferri.
english: For the Son of God, namely the Word and Wisdom of the Father, first, when He finds that power of our soul which is called reason depressed by the flesh, captive to sin, blind with ignorance, given to outward things, taking it up mercifully, raising it powerfully, instructing it prudently, drawing it inward, and using it wonderfully as a deputy for Himself, sets it as a judge for itself, so that out of reverence for the Word to which it is joined, it, accuser, witness, and judge of itself, discharges the office of Truth against itself. From this first conjunction of the Word and reason, humility is born. Then the other part, which is called the will, infected indeed with the poison of the flesh, but already examined by reason, the Holy Spirit visiting it graciously, fighting sweetly, affecting it ardently, makes it merciful: so that after the manner of a hide, which when anointed is stretched, it too, poured through with a heavenly anointing, is dilated by affection even to enemies. And so from this second conjunction of the Spirit of God and the human will, charity is made. Then both parts, namely reason and will, the one instructed by the word of truth, the other breathed upon by the spirit of truth; the one sprinkled with the hyssop of humility, the other kindled with the fire of charity; the soul now perfect, without spot because of humility, without wrinkle because of charity; when neither the will resists reason, nor reason disguises the truth, the Father joins to Himself as a glorious spouse: so that neither reason is allowed to think of itself, nor the will of the neighbor, but that blessed soul delights to say only this: “The King has brought me into His chamber.” Worthy indeed, who from the school of humility, in which she first learned under the Master the Son to enter into herself, according to the threat made to her, “If you do not know yourself, go forth and feed your kids” (Song 1:3, 7); worthy, then, to be brought by affection from that school of humility, with the Holy Spirit as guide, into the cellars of charity (which are surely to be understood as the breasts of neighbors); whence, supported with flowers and surrounded with apples, that is with good manners and holy virtues, she may at last be admitted to the King’s chamber, for love of whom she languishes. There for a little while, for about half an hour, silence being made in heaven, resting sweetly among the desired embraces, she herself sleeps, but her heart watches, by which meanwhile she searches the secrets of truth: with the memory of which she may afterwards be fed when she returns to herself. There she sees invisible things, hears unspeakable things, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. They exceed all that knowledge which night indicates to night: yet day utters the word to day, and among the wise it is lawful to speak wisdom, and to the spiritual to compare spiritual things.

chunks.latin: Ibi modicum, hora videlicet quasi dimidia, silentio facto in coelo, inter desideratos amplexus suaviter quiescens, ipsa quidem dormit, sed cor eius vigilat, quo utique interim veritatis arcana rimatur: quorum postmodum memoria statim ad se reditura pascatur. Ibi videt invisibilia, audit ineffabilia, quae non licet homini loqui. Excedunt quippe omnem illam, quam nox nocti indicat, scientiam: dies tamen diei eructat verbum, et inter sapientes sapientiam loqui et spiritualibus spiritualia licet conferri.
chunks.english: There for a little while, for about half an hour, silence being made in heaven, resting sweetly among the desired embraces, she herself sleeps, but her heart watches, by which meanwhile she searches the secrets of truth: with the memory of which she may afterwards be fed when she returns to herself. There she sees invisible things, hears unspeakable things, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. They exceed all that knowledge which night indicates to night: yet day utters the word to day, and among the wise it is lawful to speak wisdom, and to the spiritual to compare spiritual things.

heading: CAPUT VIII. Gradus iidem in raptu sancti Pauli declarantur
latin: CAPUT VIII. Gradus iidem in raptu sancti Pauli declarantur.
english: Chapter VIII. The same steps are declared in the rapture of Saint Paul.
label: CAPUT VIII. Gradus iidem in raptu sancti Pauli declarantur

chunks.latin: CAPUT VIII. Gradus iidem in raptu sancti Pauli declarantur.
chunks.english: Chapter VIII. The same steps are declared in the rapture of Saint Paul.

latin: Putas, hos gradus Paulus non transierat, qui usque ad tertium coelum se raptum fuisse testatur? (II Cor. XII, 2.) Sed quare raptum, et non potius ductum? Ut videlicet si tantus Apostolus raptum se dicit fuisse, quo nec doctus scivit, nec ductus potuit ire; me, qui procul dubio minor sum Paulo, ad tertium coelum nulla mea virtute, nullo meo labore pervenire posse praesumam: ne vel de virtute confidam, vel pro labore diffidam. Qui enim docetur aut ducitur, ex hoc ipso quod docentem vel ducentem sequitur, laborare convincitur, et aliquid ex se agit, ut ad destinatum locum vel sensum pertrabatur, ita ut dicere possit: Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum (I Cor. XV, 10). Qui vero rapitur, non suis viribus, sed alienis innixus, tanquam nescius quocunque portatur, nec de toto in se, nec de parte gloriatur, ubi nec per se, nec cum alio aliquid operatur. Ad primum itaque sive ad medium coelum ductus vel adiutus Apostolus ascendere potuit: ad tertium autem ut perveniret, rapi oportuit. Nam ad hoc et Filius legitur descendisse, ut vocaret et iuvaret ascensuros ad primum: et Spiritus sanctus missus fuisse, qui perduceret ad secundum. Pater vero, licet Filio et Spiritui sancto semper cooperetur, nunquam tamen aut de coelo descendisse, aut ad terras legitur missus fuisse. Lego certe, quod misericordia Domini plena est terra (Psal. XXXII, 5); et, Pleni sunt coeli et terra gloria tua, et multa huiusmodi. Lego et de Filio, Postquam venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum (Galat. IV, 4). Et ipse Filius loquitur de se, Spiritus Domini misit me (Isa. LXI, 1). Et per eumdem prophetam: Et nunc, inquit, Dominus misit me et Spiritus eius (Isa. XLVIII, 16). Lego et de Spiritu sancto, Paraclitus autem Spiritus sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo (Ioan. XIV, 26); et, Cum assumptus fuero, mittam vobis eum (Ioan. XVI, 7), haud dubium quin Spiritum sanctum. Patrem autem in sua persona, licet nusquam non sit, nusquam tamen invenio nisi in coelis, ut in Evangelio, Et Pater meus qui in coelis est (Matth. XXIII, 9); et in oratione, Pater noster qui es in coelis (Matth. VI, 9).
english: Do you think Paul had not passed these steps, who testifies that he was caught up as far as the third heaven? (2 Cor. 12:2.) But why “caught up,” and not rather “led”? Namely, so that if so great an Apostle says he was caught up, where he neither knew as one taught, nor could go as one led, I, who am beyond doubt less than Paul, may not presume that I can arrive at the third heaven by any virtue of mine, by any labor of mine: lest I either trust in virtue, or despair because of labor. For he who is taught or led is, by this very fact that he follows the one teaching or leading, shown to labor, and does something of himself, that he may be drawn to the destined place or meaning, so that he can say: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). But he who is caught up, leaning not on his own powers but on another’s, is carried he knows not where, and glories neither wholly in himself nor in part, where he works nothing either by himself or with another. To the first, then, or to the middle heaven the Apostle could ascend as one led or helped: but to reach the third he had to be caught up. For to this end the Son also is read to have descended, that He might call and help those who would ascend to the first; and the Holy Spirit to have been sent, who might lead to the second. But the Father, though He always cooperates with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is never read either to have descended from heaven or to have been sent to earth. I read indeed that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5); and, “Heaven and earth are full of Your glory,” and many such things. I read also of the Son, “When the fullness of time came, God sent His Son” (Gal. 4:4). And the Son Himself speaks of Himself, “The Spirit of the Lord has sent Me” (Isa. 61:1). And through the same prophet: “And now,” He says, “the Lord has sent Me, and His Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). I read also of the Holy Spirit, “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name” (John 14:26); and, “When I have been taken up, I will send Him to you” (John 16:7), no doubt the Holy Spirit. But the Father in His own person, though He is nowhere not, I nowhere find except in the heavens, as in the Gospel, “And My Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9); and in the prayer, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

latin: Unde nimirum colligo, quod quia Pater non descendit, Apostolus ut eum videret, ad tertium coelum ascendere quidem non potuit, quo tamen se raptum memoravit. Denique, Nemo ascendit in coelum, nisi qui descendit de coelo Filius hominis(Ioan. III, 13). Et ne putes de primo dictum vel secundo, dicit tibi David: A summo coelo egressio eius(Psal. XVIII, 7). Ad quod iterum non subito raptus, non furtim sublatus, sed, Videntibus, inquit, illis, id est Apostolis, elevatus est(Act. I, 9). Non sicut Elias, qui unum (IV Reg. II); non sicut Paulus, qui nullum (vix enim vel seipsum testem aut arbitrum habere potuit, ipso perhibente, Nescio, Deus scit : sed ut Omnipotens, qui quando voluit descendit, quando voluit ascendit, pro suo arbitrio arbitros et spectatores, locum et tempus, diem et horam exspectans, videntibus illis, quos scilicet tanta visione dignatur, elevatus est. Raptus est Paulus, raptus est Elias, translatus est Enoch (Eccli. XLIV, 16): Redemptor vero noster legitur elevatus, hoc est, ex seipso levatus, non aliunde adiutus. Denique non currus vehiculo, non angeli adminiculo, sed propria virtute subnixum suscepit eum nubes ab oculis eorum(Act. I, 9). Cur hoc? An fessum iuvit? an pigrum impulit? an cadentem sustinuit? Absit. Sed suscepit eum ab oculis carnalibus discipulorum: qui, etsi Christum noverant secundum carnem, sed ultra iam non noscerent. Quos ergo per humilitatem ad primum coelum Filius vocat, hos in secundo per caritatem Spiritus aggregat, ad tertium per contemplationem Pater exaltat. Primo humiliantur in veritate, et dicunt, In veritate tua humiliasti me(Psal. CXVIII, 75). Secundo congaudent veritati, et psallunt, Ecce quam bonum, et quam iucundum habitare fratres in unum?(Psal. CXXXII, 1.) De caritate quippe scriptum est, Congaudet autem, veritati(I Cor. XIII, 6). Tertio ad arcana veritatis rapiuntur, et aiunt, Secretum meum mihi, secretum meum mihi(Isa. XXIV, 16).
english: From which I gather that because the Father did not descend, the Apostle, that he might see Him, could not indeed ascend to the third heaven, to which nevertheless he recorded that he was caught up. Finally, “No one has ascended into heaven except He who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). And lest you think this said of the first or the second, David says to you: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18:7). To which again He was not suddenly caught up, not secretly taken, but “while they looked on,” it says, that is the Apostles, “He was lifted up” (Acts 1:9). Not as Elijah, who had one (2 Kings 2); not as Paul, who had none (for he could scarcely have even himself as witness or umpire, himself declaring, “I know not, God knows”); but as the Almighty, who when He willed descended, when He willed ascended, awaiting according to His own choice witnesses and spectators, place and time, day and hour, “while they looked on,” whom namely He deigns with so great a vision, was lifted up. Paul was caught up, Elijah was caught up, Enoch was translated (Sir. 44:16): but our Redeemer is read to have been lifted up, that is, raised from Himself, not helped from elsewhere. Finally, not by the vehicle of a chariot, not by the aid of an angel, but supported by His own power, “a cloud received Him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9). Why this? Did it help one weary? Did it push one slow? Did it hold up one falling? Far from it. But it received Him from the carnal eyes of the disciples: who, though they had known Christ according to the flesh, should now know Him so no longer. Those, then, whom the Son calls through humility to the first heaven, the Spirit gathers in the second through charity, the Father exalts to the third through contemplation. First they are humbled in the truth, and say, “In Your truth You have humbled me” (Ps. 118:75). Second they rejoice with the truth, and sing, “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in one” (Ps. 132:1). For of charity it is written, “It rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. 13:6). Third they are caught up to the secrets of truth, and say, “My secret to me, my secret to me” (Isa. 24:16).

heading: CAPUT IX. Gemitus et suspiria sancti Bernardi, ad Veritatem anhelantis
latin: CAPUT IX. Gemitus et suspiria sancti Bernardi, ad Veritatem anhelantis.
english: Chapter IX. The groans and sighs of Saint Bernard, panting toward the Truth.
label: CAPUT IX. Gemitus et suspiria sancti Bernardi, ad Veritatem anhelantis

chunks.latin: CAPUT IX. Gemitus et suspiria sancti Bernardi, ad Veritatem anhelantis.
chunks.english: Chapter IX. The groans and sighs of Saint Bernard, panting toward the Truth.

latin: Sed quid ego miser superflua magis loquacitate, quam spiritus vivacitate duos coelos superiores percurro, qui manibus pedibusque repens adhuc sub inferiore laboro? Ad quod tamen iam, ipso iuvante, quo et vocante, mihi scalam erexi. Illic siquidem iter est, quo ostendat mihi salutare Dei. Iam Dominum desuper innixum suspicio, iam ad vocem veritatis exsulto. Vocavit me, et ego respondi illi: Operi manuum tuarum porriges dexteram (Iob XIV, 15). Tu quidem, Domine, gressus meos dinumeras, sed ego lentus ascensor, fessus viator, diverticula quaero. Vae mihi, si tenebrae me comprehendant, aut si mea fuga fiat in hieme, vel in Sabbato: dum nunc ad lucem, cum tempus acceptabile et dies salutis sunt, proficisci dissimulo. Quid moror? Ora pro me, fili, frater, socie, et particeps profectus mei, si quis est, in Domino. Ora Omnipotentem, quatenus sic pigrum roboret pedem, ut tamen non veniat mihi pes superbiae. Etsi enim pes piger, ut ad veritatis gradum ascendat, idoneus non est: tolerabilior tamen est isto, qui in ea stare non potest, ut habes ibi: Expulsi sunt, nec potuerunt stare (Psal. XXXV, 12, 13).
english: But why do I, a wretch, with superfluous talkativeness more than with liveliness of spirit, run through the two higher heavens, who still labor under the lower, creeping on hands and feet? To which nevertheless already, with Him helping by whom I am also called, I have raised a ladder for myself. For there is the way by which He may show me the salvation of God. Already I look up to the Lord leaning from above, already I exult at the voice of truth. He called me, and I answered Him: “You will stretch out Your right hand to the work of Your hands” (Job 14:15). You indeed, O Lord, number my steps, but I, a slow climber, a weary traveler, look for byways. Woe to me, if darkness overtake me, or if my flight be in winter, or on the Sabbath: while now, when it is the acceptable time and the day of salvation, I put off setting out toward the light. Why do I delay? Pray for me, son, brother, companion, and sharer of my progress, if there is any, in the Lord. Pray the Almighty, that He may so strengthen the sluggish foot that yet the foot of pride may not come to me. For though a sluggish foot is not fit to climb the step of truth, it is still more tolerable than that which cannot stand in it, as you have there: “They were cast out, and could not stand” (Ps. 35:12–13).

latin: Et hoc quidem de superbis. Sed quid de illorum capite? quid de illo, qui dicitur rex super omnes filios superbiae? (Iob. XLI, 25.) Et ipse, inquit, in veritate non stetit (Ioan. VIII, 44): et alibi, Videbam Satanam sicut fulgur cadentem de coelo (Luc. X, 18). Quare hoc, nisi propter superbiam? Vae mihi, si et me viderit, qui alta a longe cognoscit, superbientem; et illam in me terribilem intonet vocem: Tu quidem filius Excelsi eras, sed sicut homo morieris, et sicut unus de principibus cades (Psal. LXXXI, 6, 7). Quis non ab huius tonitrui voce formidet? O quam salubrius ad tactum angeli nervus femoris Iacob emarcuit (Gen. XXXII, 25), quam angeli superbientis intumuit, evanuit, ruit. Utinam et meum nervum angelus tangat ut marcescat, si forte ex hac infirmitate incipiam proficere, qui ex mea firmitate non possum nisi deficere. Lego profecto: Quod infirmum est Dei, fortius est hominibus (I Cor. I, 25). Sic quoque Apostolus de suo nervo conquestus, quem angelus non Domini, sed Satanae colaphizabat, responsum audivit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea; nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Quae virtus? Ipse Apostolus respondeat: Libenter gloriabor in infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me virtus Christi (II Cor. XII, 9). Sed nondum forsitan intelligis, de qua specialiter dixerit, quia Christus omnes virtutes habuit. Sed, cum omnes habuerit, prae omnibus tamen unam, id est humilitatem, nobis in se commendavit, cum ait: Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Matth. XI, 29).
english: And this indeed of the proud. But what of their head? What of him who is called king over all the children of pride? (Job 41:25.) “And he,” it says, “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44); and elsewhere, “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Why this, if not because of pride? Woe to me, if He also who knows high things from afar should see me prideful, and thunder upon me that terrible voice: “You were indeed a son of the Most High, but you shall die like a man, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:6–7). Who would not fear at the voice of this thunder? O how much more healthfully did Jacob’s sinew of the thigh wither at the angel’s touch (Gen. 32:25), than did that of the proud angel swell, vanish, and fall. Would that an angel might touch my sinew also, that it may wither, if perhaps from this infirmity I may begin to advance, who from my own firmness can only fail. I read indeed: “The weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). So also the Apostle, complaining of his own sinew, which an angel not of the Lord but of Satan was buffeting, heard the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in infirmity.” What power? But though He had them all, yet above all He commended to us in Himself one, that is humility, when He said: “Learn from Me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

VIII, 44): et alibi, Videbam Satanam sicut fulgur cadentem de coelo (Luc. X, 18). Quare hoc, nisi propter superbiam?

latin: Libenter igitur et ego, Domine Iesu, gloriabor, si potero, in mea infirmitate, in mei nervi contractione, ut tua virtus, id est humilitas, perficiatur in me. Nam sufficit mihi gratia tua, cum defecerit virtus mea. Pedem profecto gratiae fortiter figens, et meum qui infirmus est, leniter trahens, securus ascendam per scalam humilitatis: donec veritati adhaerens, ad latitudinem transeam caritatis. Tunc psallam cum gratiarum actione, et dicam: Statuisti in loco spatioso pedes meos (Psal. XXX, 9). Sic arcta via cautius inceditur strictim, sic ardua scala tutius pedetentim ascenditur; sic miro modo licet pigrius, ad veritatem tamen firmius claudicando ascenditur. Sed, heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est? (Psal. CXIX, 5.) Quis dabit mihi pennas sicut columbae, quibus celerius volem ad veritatem, ut iam requiescam in caritate? (Psal. LIV, 7.) Quae quoniam desunt, deduc me, Domine, in via tua, et ingrediar in veritate tua, et veritas liberabit me. Vae mihi quod de illa descendi. Nisi enim prius leviter, inaniter descendissem; in ascendendo tamdiu, tam graviter non laborassem. Sed quid dico, Descendi? nam fortasse rectius Cecidi dixerim. Nisi quia forte sicut nemo repente fit summus, sed gradatim quisque ascendit; sic nemo repente fit pessimus, sed paulatim descendit. english: Gladly therefore I also, Lord Jesus, will glory, if I can, in my infirmity, in the shrinking of my sinew, that Your power, that is humility, may be perfected in me. For Your grace is sufficient for me, when my own power has failed. Setting the foot of grace firmly, and gently drawing mine which is weak, I will climb securely by the ladder of humility: until, clinging to the truth, I pass over to the breadth of charity. Then I will sing with thanksgiving, and say: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9). So a narrow way is more cautiously walked strictly, so a steep ladder is more safely climbed step by step; so in a wondrous manner, though more slowly, one climbs more firmly to the truth by limping. But woe is me, because my sojourning is prolonged! (Ps. 119:5.) Who will give me wings like a dove, with which I may fly more quickly to the truth, that I may already rest in charity? (Ps. 54:7.) And since they are lacking, lead me, O Lord, in Your way, and I will enter into Your truth, and the truth will set me free. Woe to me that I descended from it. For unless I had first descended lightly, emptily, I would not have labored so long, so heavily, in climbing. But why do I say, “I descended”? For perhaps I would more rightly have said, “I fell.” Except that, as no one suddenly becomes the highest, but each climbs by steps, so no one suddenly becomes the worst, but descends little by little. Otherwise how will that stand: “The wicked man is proud all the days of his life”? (Job 15:20.) Finally there are ways that seem good to men, and yet lead to evil.

latin: Est ergo via descensionis, sicut et ascensionis. Et via est ad bonum, et via est ad malum. Cave malam, elige bonam. Si per te non potes, ora cum propheta, et dic: Viam iniquitatis amove a me. Quomodo? Et de lege tua miserere mei; illa scilicet lege, quam dedisti delinquentibus in via, id est derelinquentibus veritatem, de quibus unus ego sum, qui vere a veritate cecidi. Sed numquid qui cadit, non adiiciet ut resurgat? Propter hoc viam veritatis elegi, qua ascendam humiliatus, unde superbiendo descendi. Ascendam, inquam, et psallam: Bonum mihi, Domine, quod humiliasti me; bonum mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti (Psal. CXVIII, 29, 30, 71, 72). Duas tibi vias videtur David proposuisse, sed unam noveris esse; ipsam tamen a se diversam, et diversis nominibus appellatam, aut iniquitatis propter descendentes, aut veritatis propter ascendentes: quia et iidem gradus sunt ascendentium in solium, et descendentium; et eadem via accedentium ad civitatem, et recedentium; et unum ostium est ingredientium domum, et egredientium. Per unam denique scalam ascendentes Angeli, et descendentes Iacob apparuerunt (Gen. XXVIII, 12). Quo spectant haec? Ut videlicet si ad veritatem redire cupis, non necesse sit viam quaerere novam quam non nosti, sed notam qua descendisti: quatenus reciprocis gressibus tua ipse vestigia sequens, per eosdem gradus humiliatus ascendas, per quos superbiendo descenderas: ita ut qui duodecimus superbiae fuit descendenti, primus humilitatis sit ascendenti; undecimus, inveniatur secundus; decimus, tertius; nonus, quartus; octavus, quintus; septimus, sextus; sextus, septimus; quintus, octavus; quartus, nonus; tertius, decimus; secundus, undecimus; primus, duodecimus. Quibus superbiae gradibus in te inventis, imo recognitis, iam non laboras in quaerendo viam humilitatis.
english: There is therefore a way of descent, as of ascent. And there is a way to good, and a way to evil. Beware the evil, choose the good. If you cannot of yourself, pray with the prophet, and say: “Remove from me the way of iniquity.” How? “And of Your law have mercy on me”; that law, namely, which You gave to those who go astray in the way, that is who abandon the truth, of whom I am one, who truly fell from the truth. But shall he who falls not add that he may rise again? For this I have chosen the way of truth, by which I may climb, humbled, from where I descended by pride. I will climb, I say, and I will sing: “It is good for me, O Lord, that You have humbled me; the law of Your mouth is good to me above thousands of gold and silver” (Ps. 118:29, 30, 71, 72). David seems to have set two ways before you, but you should know they are one; yet diverse from itself, and called by diverse names, either of iniquity because of those descending, or of truth because of those ascending: because the same steps belong to those climbing to a throne and to those descending; and the same way to those approaching a city and to those departing; and one door is of those entering a house and of those going out. Finally, by one ladder the angels appeared to Jacob, ascending and descending (Gen. 28:12). To what do these things look? Namely, that if you desire to return to the truth, it is not necessary to seek a new way which you do not know, but the known way by which you descended: so that, following your own footprints with reciprocal steps, you may climb by the same steps, humbled, by which you had descended in pride: so that what was the twelfth of pride for the one descending may be the first of humility for the one ascending; the eleventh is found the second; the tenth, the third; the ninth, the fourth; the eighth, the fifth; the seventh, the sixth; the sixth, the seventh; the fifth, the eighth; the fourth, the ninth; the third, the tenth; the second, the eleventh; the first, the twelfth. When these steps of pride have been found in you, or rather recognized, you no longer labor in seeking the way of humility.

heading: CAPUT X. De primo superbiae gradu, qui est curiositas
latin: CAPUT X. De primo superbiae gradu, qui est curiositas.
english: Chapter X. On the first step of pride, which is curiosity.
label: CAPUT X. De primo superbiae gradu, qui est curiositas

chunks.latin: CAPUT X. De primo superbiae gradu, qui est curiositas.
chunks.english: Chapter X. On the first step of pride, which is curiosity.

latin: Primus itaque superbiae gradus est curiositas. Hanc autem talibus indiciis deprehendes. Si videris monachum, de quo prius bene confidebas, ubicunque stat, ambulat, sedet, oculis incipientem vagari, caput erectum, aures portare suspensas; e motibus exterioris hominis interiorem immutatum agnoscas. Vir quippe perversus annuit oculo, terit pede, digito loquitur (Prov. VI, 12, 13); et ex insolenti corporis motu, recens animae morbus deprehenditur: quam, dum a sui circumspectione torpescit incuria sui, curiosam in alios facit. Quia enim seipsam ignorat, foras mittitur, ut haedos pascat (Cantic. I, 7). Haedos quippe, qui peccatum significant, recte oculos auresque appellaverim: quoniam sicut mors per peccatum in orbem, sic per has fenestras intrat ad mentem. In his ergo pascendis se occupat curiosus, dum scire non curat qualem se reliquerit intus. Et vere si te vigilanter, homo, attendas, mirum est si ad aliud unquam intendas. Audi, curiose, Salomonem; audi, stulte, Sapientem. Omni custodia, inquit, custodi cor tuum (Prov. IV, 23): ut omnes videlicet sensus tui vigilent ad id, unde vita procedit, custodiendum. Quo enim a te, o curiose, recedis? Cui te interim committis? Utquid audes oculos levare ad coelum, qui peccasti in coelum? Terram intuere, ut cognoscas teipsum. Ipsa te tibi repraesentabit, quia terra es, et in terram ibis.
english: The first step of pride, then, is curiosity. You will detect it by such signs as these. If you see a monk, of whom you formerly had good confidence, wherever he stands, walks, sits, beginning to wander with his eyes, his head erect, carrying his ears cocked: from the motions of the outward man you may recognize that the inward has been changed. For a perverse man winks with the eye, scrapes with the foot, speaks with the finger (Prov. 6:12–13); and from the insolent motion of the body a recent disease of the soul is detected: which, while by carelessness of itself it grows sluggish in watching itself, makes it curious toward others. For because it does not know itself, it is sent outside to feed the kids (Song 1:7). Kids, which signify sin, I would rightly call the eyes and ears: because as death entered the world through sin, so through these windows it enters the mind. In feeding these, then, the curious man occupies himself, while he does not care to know what he has left within. And truly, if you attended to yourself vigilantly, O man, it is a wonder if you would ever attend to anything else. Hear, O curious one, Solomon; hear, O fool, the Wise Man. “With all watchfulness,” he says, “keep your heart” (Prov. 4:23): that all your senses may watch over that from which life proceeds. For whither, O curious one, do you withdraw from yourself? To whom do you meanwhile commit yourself? Why do you dare to lift your eyes to heaven, you who have sinned against heaven? Look upon the earth, that you may know yourself. It will represent you to yourself, because you are earth, and to earth you will go.

Look upon the earth, that you may know yourself. It will represent you to yourself, because you are earth, and to earth you will go.

latin: Duabus tamen ex causis inculpabiliter oculos levas, ut vel petas auxilium, vel impendas. Levavit oculos David in montes, ut peteret (Psal. CXX, 1): levavit et Dominus super turbas, ut impenderet (Ioan. VI, 5). Alter miserabiliter, alter misericorditer, ambo inculpabiliter. Tu quoque si locum, tempus et causam considerans, tua vel fratris necessitate oculos levas; non solum non culpo, sed et plurimum laudo. Hoc enim excusat miseria, illud commendat misericordia. Sin alias, non Prophetae, non Domini, sed Dinae aut Evae, imo ipsius Satanae imitatorem te dixerim. Dina namque dum ad pascendos haedos egreditur, ipsa patri, et sua sibi virginitas rapitur (Gen. XXXIV, 1, 2). O Dina, quid necesse est ut videas mulieres alienigenas? Qua necessitate? qua utilitate? An sola curiositate? Etsi tu otiose vides, sed non otiose videris. Tu curiose spectas, sed curiosius spectaris. Quis crederet tunc illam tuam curiosam otiositatem, vel otiosam curiositatem, fore post sic non otiosam, sed tibi, tuis, hostibusque tam perniciosam?
english: Yet for two reasons you lift your eyes blamelessly, either to ask help or to give it. David lifted his eyes to the mountains, that he might ask (Ps. 120:1): and the Lord lifted His over the crowds, that He might give (John 6:5). The one miserably, the other mercifully, both blamelessly. You too, if considering place, time, and cause, you lift your eyes for your own need or your brother’s, I not only do not blame, but even greatly praise. For misery excuses the one, mercy commends the other. Otherwise I would call you an imitator not of the Prophet, not of the Lord, but of Dinah or of Eve, or rather of Satan himself. For Dinah, while she goes out to feed the kids, her virginity is taken from her father, and her own from herself (Gen. 34:1–2). O Dinah, what need is there that you see the women of another people? By what necessity? By what usefulness? Or by curiosity alone? Even if you look idly, you are not idly looked at. You gaze curiously, but you are gazed at more curiously. Who would then have believed that that curious idleness of yours, or idle curiosity, would afterwards be so not idle, but so pernicious to you, to yours, and to your enemies?

latin: Tu quoque, o Eva, in paradiso posita es, ut cum viro tuo opereris et custodias illum: si iniunctum perfeceris, quandoque transitura ad melius, ubi nec opus sit te in aliquo opere occupari, nec de custodia sollicitari. Omne lignum paradisi tibi conceditur ad vescendum, praeter illud, quod dicitur scientiae boni et mali (Gen. II, 15-17). Si enim caetera bona sunt, et sapiunt bonum, quid est opus edere de ligno, quod sapit etiam malum? Non plus sapere, quam oportet sapere (Rom. XII, 3). Sapere enim malum, sapere non est, sed desipere. Serva ergo commissum, exspecta promissum; cave prohibitum, ne perdas concessum. Quid tuam mortem tam intente intueris? Quid illo tam crebro vagantia lumina iacis? Quid spectare libet, quod manducare non licet? Oculos, inquis, tendo, non manum. Non est interdictum ne videam, sed ne comedam. An non licet oculos quo volo levare, quos Deus in mea posuit potestate? Ad quod Apostolus: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt (I Cor. VI, 12). Etsi culpa non est, culpae tamen indicium est. Nisi enim mens minus se curiose servaret, tua curiositas tempus vacuum non haberet. Etsi culpa non est, culpae tamen occasio est, et indicium commissae, et causa est committendae. Te enim intenta ad aliud, latenter interim in cor tuum serpens illabitur, blande alloquitur. Blanditiis rationem, mendaciis timorem compescit. Nequaquam, inquiens, morieris (Gen. III, 4). Auget curam, dum incitat gulam: acuit curiositatem, dum suggerit cupiditatem. Offert tandem prohibitum, et aufert concessum: porrigit pomum, et subripit paradisum. Hauris virus peritura, et perituros paritura. Perit salus, non destitit partus. Nascimur, morimur: ideoque nascimur morituri, quia prius morimur nascituri. Propterea grave iugum super omnes filios tuos usque in hodiernum diem.
english: You too, O Eve, were placed in paradise, that you might work with your husband and keep it: if you fulfill what was enjoined, to pass over at some time to something better, where there will be no need for you to be occupied in any work, nor to be anxious about custody. Every tree of paradise is granted you for eating, except that which is called of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:15–17). For if the rest are good, and taste of good, what need is there to eat of the tree which tastes also of evil? “Not to be wiser than it is fitting to be wise” (Rom. 12:3). For to taste evil is not to be wise, but to be foolish. Keep therefore what was committed, wait for what was promised; beware what was forbidden, lest you lose what was granted. Why do you gaze so intently on your own death? Why do you cast wandering lights so often there? Why does it please you to look at what it is not lawful to eat? “I stretch out my eyes,” you say, “not my hand. It is not forbidden that I see, but that I eat. May I not lift my eyes where I will, which God placed in my power?” To which the Apostle: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. 6:12). Even if it is not a fault, it is nevertheless a sign of a fault. For unless the mind kept itself less curiously, your curiosity would not have empty time. Even if it is not a fault, it is nevertheless an occasion of a fault, and a sign of one committed, and a cause of one to be committed. For while you are intent on something else, the serpent meanwhile secretly glides into your heart, addresses you blandly. He checks reason with blandishments, fear with lies. “By no means,” he says, “shall you die” (Gen. 3:4). He increases care, while he incites the gullet: he sharpens curiosity, while he suggests desire. At last he offers what was forbidden, and takes away what was granted: he holds out the apple, and snatches paradise. You drink the poison, about to perish, and about to bear those who will perish. Salvation perishes, birth does not cease. We are born, we die: and therefore we are born to die, because we first die about to be born. Therefore a heavy yoke is upon all your children even to this day.

latin: Sed et tu, signaculum similitudinis, non in paradiso, sed in deliciis paradisi Dei positus es (Ezech. XXVIII, 12, 13). Quid amplius quaerere debes? Plenus ergo sapientia, et perfectus decore, altiora te ne quaesieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris. Sta in te, ne cadas a te, si ambulas in magnis et in mirabilibus super te. Sed quid interim ex obliquo intendis ad aquilonem? Iam te video, iam te perspicio nescio quae supra te curiosius alta rimantem. Ponam, inquit, sedem meam ad aquilonem (Isa. XIV, 13). Caeteris astantibus coelicolis, dum tu solus sedere affectas, fratrum concordiam, totius coelestis patriae pacem, ipsius, quantum in te est, quietem Trinitatis infestas. Quo te tua, miser, curiositas ducit, ut praesumptione singulari non dubites civibus scandalum, iniuriam facere Regi? Millia millium ministrant ei, et decies centena millia assistunt ei (Dan VII, 10), ubi nemo sedere perhibetur, nisi solus is qui sedet super Cherubim, cui a caeteris ministratur: et tu nescio quae prae caeteris perspiciendo differentius, curiosius inquirendo, irreverentius pervadendo, sedem tibi collocas in coelo, ut sis similis Altissimo? Quo fine? qua fiducia? Metire, insipiens, vires, pensa finem, excogita modum. Sciente hoc Altissimo praesumis, an nesciente? volente, an non volente? Sed quomodo malum quodcunque machinaris, aut velle, aut ignorare potest, cuius optima voluntas, cuius perfecta scientia est? Numquid autem et scire, et nolle non dubitas, sed non posse resistere putas? At vero nisi te conditum esse dubitaveris, dubitare te non crediderim de omnipotentia, sive de omnimoda scientia ac bonitate Conditoris, qui te de nihilo potuit, talem scivit, tantum condere voluit. Quomodo ergo Deum consentire aestimas, quod fieri nolit, ac refellere possit? An forte in te video compleri, imo a te initiari, quod post te, et per te a tui similibus in terris frequentatum solet vulgariter dici: Privatus dominus temerarios nutrit ? An oculos tuus nequam est, quia ille bonus? De cuius bonitate dum fiduciam nefariam sumis, factus es et contra scientiam impudens, et contra potentiam audax.
english: But you also, O seal of likeness, were placed not in paradise, but in the delights of the paradise of God (Ezek. 28:12–13). What more ought you to seek? Full therefore of wisdom, and perfect in beauty, seek not things higher than yourself, and search not things stronger than yourself. Stand in yourself, lest you fall from yourself, if you walk in great things and in wonders above yourself. But why do you meanwhile look aslant toward the north? Already I see you, already I perceive you searching I know not what high things above yourself more curiously. “I will set,” he says, “my seat toward the north” (Isa. 14:13). While the other heavenly citizens stand by, you alone affect to sit, and you attack the concord of the brothers, the peace of the whole heavenly country, and, as far as in you lies, the quiet of the Trinity itself. Whither does your curiosity, wretch, lead you, that by a singular presumption you do not hesitate to make scandal for the citizens, injury to the King? Thousands of thousands minister to Him, and ten times a hundred thousand stand before Him (Dan. 7:10), where no one is said to sit except He alone who sits above the Cherubim, to whom the rest minister: and you, looking more distinctly than the rest I know not at what, inquiring more curiously, invading more irreverently, set a seat for yourself in heaven, that you may be like the Most High? With what end? With what confidence? Measure, O fool, your strength, weigh the end, think out the measure. Do you presume this with the Most High knowing, or not knowing? willing, or not willing? But how can He either will, or be ignorant of, whatever evil you devise, whose will is best, whose knowledge is perfect? Or do you not doubt that He both knows and is unwilling, but think He cannot resist? Yet unless you doubt that you were created, I would not believe you doubt the omnipotence, or the complete knowledge and goodness of the Creator, who could from nothing, knew how to make you such, willed to make you so great. How then do you suppose God consents to what He does not will to be done, and can refuse? Or perhaps I see fulfilled in you, or rather begun by you, what after you, and through you by those like you on earth, is commonly said: “A private lord nourishes rash men”? Or is your eye evil, because He is good? From whose goodness, while you take a wicked confidence, you have been made both shameless against knowledge and bold against power.

latin: Hoc est enim, o impie, hoc est quod cogitas; haec est iniquitas, quam meditaris in cubili tuo, et dicis: Putas Creator opus suum destruat? Scio quidem quia non latet Deum qualiscunque cogitatio mea: Deus enim est. Nec placet ei talis cogitatio mea, quia bonus est. Sed nec si velit effugiam manus eius, quia potens est. Nunquid tamen mihi timendum est? Si enim cum bonus sit, non potest illi placere malum meum, quanto minus suum? Meum quippe dixerim contra eius voluntatem aliquid velle: suum autem, si vindicet sese. Tam ergo quodeunque scelus non valet velle ulcisci, quam nec vult, nec valet sua bonitate privari. Fallis te, miser, fallis te, non Deum. Te, inquam, fallis, et mentitur iniquitas sibi, non Deo. Dolose quidem agis, sed in conspectu eius. Te ergo fallis, non Deum. Et quia de magno eius bono in te, tu magnum in eum excogitas malum, merito iniquitas tua invenitur ad odium. Quae maior namque iniquitas, quam ut inde a te Creator contemnatur, unde plus amari merebatur? Quae maior iniquitas, quam cum de potentia Dei non dubites, quin te scilicet destruere possit qui condere potuit; confisus tamen de multa eius dulcedine, qua speras eum nolle vindicare cum possit; mala pro bonis, odium pro dilectione retribuas?
english: For this, O impious one, this is what you think; this is the iniquity which you meditate on your bed, and you say: “Do you think the Creator will destroy His own work? I know indeed that no thought of mine, of whatever kind, is hidden from God: for He is God. Nor does such a thought of mine please Him, because He is good. But neither, if He should will, would I escape His hand, because He is powerful. Yet is it to be feared by me? For if, since He is good, my evil cannot please Him, how much less His own? Mine, indeed, I would call the willing of something against His will: His, if He should avenge Himself. Therefore whatever crime He cannot will to avenge, as He neither wills nor can be deprived of His own goodness. You deceive yourself, wretch, you deceive yourself, not God. You, I say, deceive yourself, and iniquity lies to itself, not to God. You act indeed deceitfully, but in His sight. You therefore deceive yourself, not God. And because from His great good toward you you devise a great evil against Him, rightly is your iniquity found unto hatred. For what greater iniquity, than that the Creator should be despised by you for that very thing for which He deserved to be more loved? What greater iniquity, than that, while you do not doubt of the power of God—that He who could create can destroy you—yet, trusting in His great sweetness, by which you hope He is unwilling to avenge though He can, you repay evils for goods, hatred for love?

chunks.latin: Et quia de magno eius bono in te, tu magnum in eum excogitas malum, merito iniquitas tua invenitur ad odium. Quae maior namque iniquitas, quam ut inde a te Creator contemnatur, unde plus amari merebatur? Quae maior iniquitas, quam cum de potentia Dei non dubites, quin te scilicet destruere possit qui condere potuit; confisus tamen de multa eius dulcedine, qua speras eum nolle vindicare cum possit; mala pro bonis, odium pro dilectione retribuas?
chunks.english: And because from His great good toward you you devise a great evil against Him, rightly is your iniquity found unto hatred. For what greater iniquity, than that the Creator should be despised by you for that very thing for which He deserved to be more loved? What greater iniquity, than that, while you do not doubt of the power of God—that He who could create can destroy you—yet, trusting in His great sweetness, by which you hope He is unwilling to avenge though He can, you repay evils for goods, hatred for love?

latin: Haec, inquam, iniquitas, non ira momentanea, sed odio digna est sempiterno, qua tuo dulcissimo et altissimo Domino, licet invito, desideras tamen ac speras aequari, quatenus semper videat quod dolcat, dum te socium habeat cum nolit, nec deiiciat cum possit; quin potius eligat ipse dolere, quam te patiatur perire; possit quidem deiicere si velit, sed prae dulcedine, ut aestimas, velle non possit. Certe si talis est qualem putas, tanto nequius agis, si non amas. Et si ille patitur aliquid fieri contra se potius, quam ipse aliquid faciat contra te; quanta malitia est, ut vel tu non parcas illi, qui sibi non parcit, parcendo tibi? Absit tamen ab eius perfectione, ut quia dulcis est, iustus non sit, quasi simul dulcis et iustus esse non possit: cum melior sit iusta dulcedo, quam remissa; imo virtus non sit dulcedo sine iustitia. Quia igitur gratuitae Dei bonitati, qua gratis factus es, ingratus existis, iustitiam vero quam expertus non es, non metuis; ideoque audacter committis culpam, de qua falso tibi promittis impunitatem: iam ecce iustum senties, quem bonum nosti, cadens in foveam, quam paras auctori: ut dum scilicet talem in eum poenam machinaris, qua tamen valeat carere si velit, sed ut putas non valeat velle; et ideo nec carere ea utique bonitate, qua neminem expertus es illum punisse: talem iustus Deus iustissime in te retorqueat poenam, qui nec valet, nec debet pati suam impune bonitatem offendi: sic utique temperans in vindicta sententiam, ut, si velis resipiscere, non neget veniam; secundum tamen duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, non possis velle, et ideo nec poena carere.
english: This iniquity, I say, is not a momentary anger, but worthy of everlasting hatred, by which you desire and hope to be equaled to your most sweet and most high Lord, though against His will, so that He may always see what grieves Him, while He has you as a companion when He does not will, and does not cast you down when He can; that He would rather choose to grieve Himself than suffer you to perish; He could indeed cast down if He willed, but, as you suppose, because of sweetness He could not will. Surely if He is such as you think, you act so much the more wickedly if you do not love. And if He suffers something to be done against Himself rather than Himself do something against you: what great malice is it, that you should not even spare Him who does not spare Himself in sparing you? Yet far be it from His perfection that, because He is sweet, He should not be just, as if He could not be at once sweet and just: since a just sweetness is better than a remiss one; rather, sweetness without justice is not a virtue. Because therefore you are ungrateful to the free goodness of God, by which you were made freely, and you do not fear the justice which you have not experienced; and so you boldly commit a fault for which you falsely promise yourself impunity: now behold, you shall feel as just Him whom you knew as good, falling into the pit which you prepare for the Author: so that while you devise against Him a punishment which He can yet be without if He wills, but, as you think, cannot will to be without, and therefore cannot be without that goodness by which you have never found Him to have punished anyone: such a punishment let the just God most justly turn back upon you, who neither can nor ought to suffer His goodness to be offended with impunity: so tempering the sentence in vengeance that, if you will to come to your senses, He does not deny pardon; yet according to your hardness and impenitent heart you cannot will, and therefore cannot be without the punishment.

latin: Sed iam audi calumniam: Coelum, inquit, mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum (Isa. LXVI, 1). Non dixit, Oriens, aut Occidens, aut Una aliqua coeli plaga: sed, Totum coelum mihi sedes est. Non potes ergo in parte sedere coeli, cum ille totum elegerit sibi. In terra non potes, quia scabellum pedum eius est. Terra etenim locus solidus est, ubi sedet Ecclesia, fundata supra firmam petram. Quid facies? E coelo pulsus, in terra remanere non potes. Elige ergo tibi in aere locum, non ad sedendum, sed ad volandum: ut qui tentasti concutere statum aeternitatis, poenam sentias propriae fluctuationis. Te ergo fluctuante inter coelum et terram, sedet Dominus super solium excelsum et elevatum, et plena est omnis terra maiestate eius (Isa. VI, 3), ut nusquam nisi in aere invenias locum.
english: But now hear the claim: “Heaven,” He says, “is My seat, and the earth the footstool of My feet” (Isa. 66:1). He did not say, East, or West, or some one region of heaven: but, “The whole heaven is My seat.” You cannot therefore sit in a part of heaven, when He has chosen the whole for Himself. On earth you cannot, because it is the footstool of His feet. For earth is a solid place, where the Church sits, founded upon a firm rock. What will you do? Driven from heaven, you cannot remain on earth. Choose therefore for yourself a place in the air, not for sitting, but for flying: so that you who tried to shake the state of eternity may feel the punishment of your own fluctuation. While you then fluctuate between heaven and earth, the Lord sits upon a throne high and lifted up, and the whole earth is full of His majesty (Isa. 6:3), so that nowhere except in the air may you find a place.

latin: Seraphim namque aliis quidem alis suae contemplationis de throno ad scabellum, de scabello ad thronum volantia, aliis caput Domini pedesque velantia, ad hoc ibi posita puto, ut sicut homini peccanti paradisi per Cherubin prohibetur ingressus, ita et per Seraphin tuae curiositati modus imponatur : quatenus nec coeli iam magis impudenter, quam prudenter arcana rimeris, nec Ecclesiae mysteria cognoscas in terris; sed solis contentus sis cordibus superborum, qui nec in terra dignantur esse sicut caeteri hominum, nec sicut Angeli volant ad coelum. Licet vero et caput in coelo, et pedes in terra a te abscondantur; quiddam tamen tibi medium videndum ad invidendum duntaxat permittitur: dum suspensus in aere, descendentes quidem per te, et ascendentes Angelos intueris; sed quid vel audiant in coelis, vel nuntient terris, penitus nescis.
english: For the Seraphim, flying with some wings of their contemplation from the throne to the footstool, from the footstool to the throne, and covering with others the head of the Lord and His feet, I suppose are placed there for this, that as for the sinning man entrance to paradise is forbidden by the Cherubim, so by the Seraphim a limit may be set to your curiosity: so that you may neither search the secrets of heaven now more shamelessly than prudently, nor know the mysteries of the Church on earth; but be content only with the hearts of the proud, who neither deign to be on earth like the rest of men, nor fly to heaven like the angels. Though the head in heaven and the feet on earth are hidden from you, yet something in the middle is permitted you to see, only that you may envy: while, suspended in the air, you look upon the angels descending through you and ascending; but what they either hear in heaven or announce on earth, you wholly do not know.

latin: O Lucifer, qui mane oriebaris, imo non iam lucifer, sed noctifer, aut etiam mortifer, rectus cursus tuus erat ab oriente ad meridiem, et tu praepostero ordine tendis ad aquilonem? Quanto magis ad alta festinas, tanto celerius ad occasum declinas. Velim tamen curiosius, o curiose, intentionem tuae curiositatis inquirere. Ponam, inquit, sedem meam ad aquilonem (Isa. XIV, 13). Nec aquilonem hunc corporalem, nec sedem hanc (cum sis spiritus) intelligo materialem. Puto autem per aquilonem, reprobandos homines fuisse designatos; per sedem, potestatem in illos. Quos utique in praescientia Dei, quanto ei vicinior, tanto caeteris perspicacior praevidens, nullo quidem sapientiae radio coruscantes, nullo spiritus amore ferventes, velut vacuum repereris locum, affectasti super illos dominium, quos quadam tuae astutiae claritate perfunderes, tuae malitiae aestibus inflammares: ut quomodo Altissimus sua sapientia ac bonitate omnibus filiis obedientiae praeerat, ita et tu super omnes filios superbiae rex constitutus, tua eos astuta malitia, ac malitiosa astutia regeres, per quod Altissimo similis esses. Sed miror cum in praesentia Dei tuum praevideris principatum, cur non in eadem praevidisti et praecipitium? Nam si praevidisti, quae insania fuit, ut cum tanta miseria cuperes principari, ut malles misere praeesse, quam feliciter subesse? An non expediebat participem esse plagarum illarum luminosarum, quam principem tenebrarum harum? Sed credibilius est, quod non praevidisti: aut propter illam causam, quam superius dixi, quia Dei bonitatem attendens, dixisti in corde tuo. Non requiret (Psal. X, 13), propter quod, o impie, Deum irritasti; aut quia viso principatu, statim in oculo superbiae trabes excrevit, qua interposita casum videre non potuisti.
english: O Lucifer, who rose in the morning, or rather no longer Lucifer, but night-bearer, or even death-bearer, your course was straight from the east to the south, and you in a reversed order tend to the north? The more you hasten to the heights, the more swiftly you decline to the setting. Yet I would inquire more curiously, O curious one, into the intention of your curiosity. “I will set,” he says, “my seat toward the north” (Isa. 14:13). I do not understand this north as bodily, nor this seat (since you are a spirit) as material. But I think that by the north reprobate men were designated; by the seat, power over them. Whom, in the foreknowledge of God, as much the nearer to Him, so much the more clear-sighted than the rest, seeing in advance, shining with no ray of wisdom, burning with no love of the spirit, you found as it were an empty place, and affected dominion over those whom you would pour through with a certain brightness of your cunning, inflame with the heats of your malice: so that as the Most High by His wisdom and goodness ruled all the children of obedience, so you also, made king over all the children of pride, might rule them by your cunning malice and malicious cunning, by which you would be like the Most High. But I wonder, when in the presence of God you foresaw your principality, why you did not in the same foresight foresee also your downfall. For if you foresaw it, what madness was it, that you should desire to rule with so great misery, that you should prefer to be over others miserably rather than to be under happily? Or was it not more expedient to be a partaker of those luminous plagues than a prince of these darknesses? But it is more credible that you did not foresee: either for that cause which I said above, because attending to the goodness of God you said in your heart, “He will not require it” (Ps. 10:13), for which, O impious one, you provoked God; or because, the principality being seen, at once a beam grew in the eye of pride, and with it interposed you could not see the fall.

latin: Sic Ioseph cum praevidisset exaltationem suam (Gen. XXXVII, 7-9), non tamen praescivit sui venditionem, quamvis propior esset venditio, quam exaltatio. Non quod tantum patriarcham in superbiam crediderim incidisse: sed ut eius exemplo pateat, quod hi qui futura praevident per spiritum prophetiae, etsi non omnia, non ideo tamen putandi sunt nulla praevidisse. Quod si quis contendat in eo quod somnia sua adhuc adolescentulus narrabat, quorum tunc mysterium ignorabat, vanitatem posse notari; ego tamen mysterio magis sive simplicitati pueri deputandum arbitror, quam vanitati. Quae tamen, si qua fuit, per ea quae passus legitur, potuit expiari. Nonnullis enim aliqua aliquando de se per revelationem iucunda monstrantur, quae etsi humanus animus absque ulla vanitate scire non potest, non minus ideo eveniet quod monstratum est; sic tamen ut illa vanitas impunita non sit, qua de magnitudine revelationis aut promissionis in se vel leviter exsultavit. Sicut enim medicus, non solum unguento, sed igne utitur et ferro, quo omne quod in vulnere sanando superfluum excreverit, secet et urat, ne sanitatem, quae ex unguento procedit, impediat: sic medicus animarum Deus huiusmodi animae procurat tentationes, immittit tribulationes, quibus afflicta et humiliata, gaudium vertat in luctum, revelationem putet illusionem. Unde fit ut vanitate careat, et veritas revelationis non pereat. Sic Pauli extollentia per stimulos carnis reprimitur (II Cor. XII, 7), et ipse revelationibus crebris attollitur. Sic Zachariae infidelitas linguae obligatione mulctatur (Luc. I, 20), et angeli veritas suo in tempore manifestanda non mutatur. Sic per gloriam et ignobilitatem sancti proficiunt, dum inter singularia dona quae recipiunt, communi hominum vanitate pulsari se sentiunt: ut dum per gratiam supra se aliquid cernunt, non obliviscantur quod sunt.
english: So Joseph, when he had foreseen his exaltation (Gen. 37:7–9), yet did not foresee his being sold, although the selling was nearer than the exaltation. Not that I would believe so great a patriarch fell into pride: but that by his example it may be clear that those who foresee future things by the spirit of prophecy, even if not all things, are not therefore to be thought to have foreseen nothing. But if anyone contends that vanity can be noted in this, that while still a youth he told his dreams, whose mystery he then did not know, I rather judge it to be ascribed to the mystery or to the simplicity of the boy than to vanity. Which yet, if there was any, could be expiated by the things he is read to have suffered. For to some, joyful things about themselves are sometimes shown by revelation, which, even if the human mind cannot know them without some vanity, what was shown will not therefore fail to come to pass; yet in such a way that that vanity is not unpunished, by which it even lightly exulted in itself at the greatness of the revelation or promise. For as a physician uses not only ointment but fire and iron, that he may cut and burn whatever has grown superfluous in healing a wound, lest it hinder the health which proceeds from the ointment: so God, the physician of souls, procures temptations for such a soul, sends tribulations, by which, afflicted and humbled, it may turn joy into mourning, and think the revelation an illusion. Whence it comes about that it is without vanity, and the truth of the revelation does not perish. So Paul’s elation is checked by the goads of the flesh (2 Cor. 12:7), and he himself is lifted by frequent revelations. So Zechariah’s unbelief is punished by the binding of the tongue (Luke 1:20), and the angel’s truth, to be manifested in its time, is not changed. So through glory and ignominy the saints advance, while among the singular gifts they receive they feel themselves struck by the common vanity of men: so that while by grace they discern something above themselves, they may not forget what they are.

Not that I would believe so great a patriarch fell into pride: but that by his example it may be clear that those who foresee future things by the spirit of prophecy, even if not all things, are not therefore to be thought to have foreseen nothing. chunks.latin: Quae tamen, si qua fuit, per ea quae passus legitur, potuit expiari. Nonnullis enim aliqua aliquando de se per revelationem iucunda monstrantur, quae etsi humanus animus absque ulla vanitate scire non potest, non minus ideo eveniet quod monstratum est; sic tamen ut illa vanitas impunita non sit, qua de magnitudine revelationis aut promissionis in se vel leviter exsultavit.
chunks.english: Which yet, if there was any, could be expiated by the things he is read to have suffered. For to some, joyful things about themselves are sometimes shown by revelation, which, even if the human mind cannot know them without some vanity, what was shown will not therefore fail to come to pass; yet in such a way that that vanity is not unpunished, by which it even lightly exulted in itself at the greatness of the revelation or promise.

chunks.latin: Sicut enim medicus, non solum unguento, sed igne utitur et ferro, quo omne quod in vulnere sanando superfluum excreverit, secet et urat, ne sanitatem, quae ex unguento procedit, impediat: sic medicus animarum Deus huiusmodi animae procurat tentationes, immittit tribulationes, quibus afflicta et humiliata, gaudium vertat in luctum, revelationem putet illusionem. Unde fit ut vanitate careat, et veritas revelationis non pereat.
chunks.english: For as a physician uses not only ointment but fire and iron, that he may cut and burn whatever has grown superfluous in healing a wound, lest it hinder the health which proceeds from the ointment: so God, the physician of souls, procures temptations for such a soul, sends tribulations, by which, afflicted and humbled, it may turn joy into mourning, and think the revelation an illusion.

chunks.latin: Sic Pauli extollentia per stimulos carnis reprimitur (II Cor. XII, 7), et ipse revelationibus crebris attollitur. Sic Zachariae infidelitas linguae obligatione mulctatur (Luc. I, 20), et angeli veritas suo in tempore manifestanda non mutatur. Sic per gloriam et ignobilitatem sancti proficiunt, dum inter singularia dona quae recipiunt, communi hominum vanitate pulsari se sentiunt: ut dum per gratiam supra se aliquid cernunt, non obliviscantur quod sunt.
chunks.english: Whence it comes about that it is without vanity, and the truth of the revelation does not perish. So Paul’s elation is checked by the goads of the flesh (2 Cor. 12:7), and he himself is lifted by frequent revelations. So Zechariah’s unbelief is punished by the binding of the tongue (Luke 1:20), and the angel’s truth, to be manifested in its time, is not changed. So through glory and ignominy the saints advance, while among the singular gifts they receive they feel themselves struck by the common vanity of men: so that while by grace they discern something above themselves, they may not forget what they are.

latin: Sed quid de revelationibus ad curiositatem? De quibus ut haec per excessum intermiscerem, inde occasio sumpta est, cum ostendere vellem, reprobum angelum ante casum suum sic potuisse praevidere illam, quam post accepit, in reprobos homines dominationem, ut tamen suam non praesciret damnationem. De quo etiam nonnullis quaestiunculis motis magis, quam solutis, totius disputatiunculae haec summa sit: quod per curiositatem a veritate ceciderit, quia prius spectavit curiose, quod affectavit illicite, speravit praesumptuose. Iure igitur in gradibus superbiae primum curiositas vindicat sibi, quae etiam inventa est initium esse omnis peccati. Sed nisi haec citius cohibeatur, in levitatem animi, quae secundus gradus est, cito delabitur.
english: But what have revelations to do with curiosity? From which, that I might mix these things in by a digression, occasion was taken when I wished to show that the reprobate angel, before his fall, could so have foreseen that dominion over reprobate men which he afterwards received, as yet not to have foreknown his own damnation. Of which, some little questions having been raised rather than solved, this is the sum of the whole little discussion: that he fell from the truth through curiosity, because he first looked curiously at what he affected unlawfully and hoped presumptuously. Rightly therefore among the steps of pride curiosity claims the first for itself, which has also been found to be the beginning of every sin. But unless this is quickly checked, it soon slips into lightness of mind, which is the second step.

heading: CAPUT XI. De secundo gradu superbiae, qui est levitas animi
latin: CAPUT XI. De secundo gradu superbiae, qui est levitas animi.
english: Chapter XI. On the second step of pride, which is lightness of mind.
label: CAPUT XI. De secundo gradu superbiae, qui est levitas animi

chunks.latin: CAPUT XI. De secundo gradu superbiae, qui est levitas animi.
chunks.english: Chapter XI. On the second step of pride, which is lightness of mind.

latin: Monachus enim, qui sui negligens, alios curiose circumspicit, dum quosdam suspicit superiores, quosdam despicit inferiores: et in aliis quidem videt quod invidet, in aliis quod irridet. Inde fit ut pro mobilitate oculorum levigatus animus, nulla utique sui cura aggravatus, modo per superbiam ad alta se erigat, modo per invidiam in ima demergat: nunc per invidiam nequiter tabescit, nunc per excellentiam pueriliter hilarescit. In altero nequam, in altero vanus, in utroque superbus existit: quia et quod superari se dolet, et quod superare se gaudet, amor propriae excellentiae facit. Has autem animi vicissitudines nunc pauca et mordacia, nunc multa et inania; nunc risu, nunc luctu plena, semper vero irrationabilia indicant verba. Compara, si vis, hos duos primos superbiae gradus supremis duobus humilitatis: et vide si non in ultimo curiositas, in penultimo levitas cohibetur. Id ipsum in caeteris reperies, si alterutrum comparentur. Sed iam ad tertium docendo, non descendendo veniamus.
english: For a monk who, neglecting himself, looks curiously at others, while he looks up to some as superiors and looks down on some as inferiors, sees in some what he envies, in others what he mocks. Hence it comes that the mind, made light by the mobility of the eyes, in no way weighed down by care of itself, now by pride raises itself to the heights, now by envy sinks itself to the depths: now by envy it wastes away wickedly, now by excellence it grows merry childishly. In the one it is wicked, in the other vain, in both proud: because both what it grieves to be surpassed in, and what it rejoices to surpass, the love of its own excellence causes. And these vicissitudes of mind are indicated by words, now few and biting, now many and empty; now full of laughter, now of mourning, but always irrational. Compare, if you will, these first two steps of pride with the last two of humility: and see whether curiosity is not checked in the last, lightness in the last but one. You will find the same in the rest, if they are compared with one another. But now let us come to the third by teaching, not by descending.

heading: CAPUT XII. De tertio gradu superbiae, qui est inepta laetitia
latin: CAPUT XII. De tertio gradu superbiae, qui est inepta laetitia.
english: Chapter XII. On the third step of pride, which is unseemly merriment.
label: CAPUT XII. De tertio gradu superbiae, qui est inepta laetitia

chunks.latin: CAPUT XII. De tertio gradu superbiae, qui est inepta laetitia.
chunks.english: Chapter XII. On the third step of pride, which is unseemly merriment.

latin: Proprium est superborum, laeta semper appetere, et tristia devitare, iuxta illud: Cor stultorum ubi laetitia (Eccle. VII, 5). Unde et monachus, qui duos iam superbiae gradus descendit, dum per curiositatem ad animi levitatem devenit, cum gaudium quod semper appetit, frequenti videt interpolari tristitia, quam de bonis alterius contrahit, impatiens suae humiliationis, fugit ad consilium falsae consolationis. Ex illa denique parte, qua sibi sua vilitas, et aliena excellentia monstratur, restringit curiositatem, ut totum se transferat in contrariam partem: quatenus in quo ipse videtur praecellere curiosius notet; in quo alter praecellit, semper dissimulet: ut dum devitat quod triste putatur, laetitia continuetur. Sicque fit ut quem sibi vicissim vindicabant gaudium et tristitia, sola possidere incipiat inepta laetitia. In hac autem, in qua tertium tibi gradum constituto, accipe quibus eam signis vel in te deprehendas, vel in altero. Illum qui eiusmodi est, aut nunquam, aut raro gementem audies, aut lacrymantem videbis. Putes, si attendas, aut sui oblitum, aut ablutum a culpis. In signis scurrilitas, in fronte hilaritas, vanitas apparet in incessu. Pronus ad iocum, facilis ac promptus in risu. Cunctis quippe quae in se contemptibilia, et ideo tristia noverat, a memoria rasis; bonisque, si qua sentit in se, adunatis vel simulatis ante oculos mentis, dum nil cogitat nisi quod libet, nec attendit si licet; iam risum tenere, iam ineptam laetitiam dissimulare non valet. Ut enim vesica collecto turgida vento, punctoque perforata exiguo, si stringitur, crepitat dum detumescit; ac ventus egrediens non passim effusus, sed strictim emissus crebros quosdam sonitus reddit: sic monachus, ubi vanis scurrilibusque cor suum cogitationibus impleverit, propter disciplinam silentii non inveniens ventus vanitatis qua plenius egrediatur, inter angustias faucium per cachinnos excutitur. Saepe vultum pudibundus abscondit, claudit labia, dentes stringit; ridet non volens, cachinnat invitus. Cumque os pugnis obstruxerit suis, per nares adhuc sternutare auditur.
english: It is proper to the proud always to seek glad things and to avoid sad ones, according to that: “The heart of fools is where there is merriment” (Eccl. 7:5). Whence also the monk who has already descended two steps of pride, when through curiosity he has come to lightness of mind, when he sees the joy which he always seeks frequently interrupted by sadness, which he contracts from another’s goods, impatient of his own humiliation, flees to the counsel of a false consolation. From that side, then, on which his own cheapness and another’s excellence are shown, he restricts curiosity, that he may transfer himself wholly to the contrary side: so that he may more curiously note that in which he himself seems to excel; and always disguise that in which another excels: so that, while he avoids what is thought sad, merriment may be continued. And so it comes about that he whom joy and sadness claimed in turn begins to be possessed by unseemly merriment alone. In this, in which I have set the third step for you, receive by what signs you may detect it either in yourself or in another. Him who is of this sort you will hear groaning never, or rarely, or see weeping. You would think, if you attended, that he had either forgotten himself, or been washed from faults. Buffoonery appears in his signs, cheerfulness in his forehead, vanity in his gait. Prone to a joke, easy and ready in laughter. For all the things he knew in himself to be contemptible, and therefore sad, having been scraped from memory, and the good things, if he feels any in himself, gathered or feigned before the eyes of the mind, while he thinks of nothing except what pleases, and does not attend whether it is lawful, he can no longer hold laughter, no longer disguise unseemly merriment. For as a bladder swollen with collected wind, and pierced with a small puncture, if it is squeezed, crackles while it is deflated, and the wind going out, not poured everywhere but emitted narrowly, returns certain frequent sounds: so a monk, when he has filled his heart with vain and scurrilous thoughts, because of the discipline of silence not finding where the wind of vanity with which he is full may go out more fully, is shaken out through the narrows of the throat in giggles. Often he hides his face ashamed, closes his lips, clenches his teeth; he laughs unwilling, giggles against his will. And when he has blocked his mouth with his fists, he is still heard to sneeze through the nostrils.
