heading: CAPUT XIII. De quarto gradu superbiae, qui est iactantia
latin: CAPUT XIII. De quarto gradu superbiae, qui est iactantia.
english: Chapter XIII. On the fourth step of pride, which is boasting.
label: CAPUT XIII. De quarto gradu superbiae, qui est iactantia

chunks.latin: CAPUT XIII. De quarto gradu superbiae, qui est iactantia.
chunks.english: Chapter XIII. On the fourth step of pride, which is boasting.

latin: At postquam vanitas crescere, et vesica grossescere coeperit, necesse est ut ampliori foramine, laxato sinu, ventositas eructetur, alioquin rumpetur. Sic monachus inepta redundante laetitia dum risu, vel signis eam aperire non sufficit, in Heliu verba prorumpit: En venter meus, quasi mustum absque spiraculo, quod novas lagunculas dirumpit (Iob. XXXII, 19). Aut loquetur ergo, aut rumpetur. Plenus est enim sermonibus, et coarctat eum spiritus uteri sui. Esurit et sitit auditores, quibus suas iactitet vanitates, quibus omne quod sentit, effundat: quibus, qualis, et quantus sit, innotescat. Inventa autem occasione loquendi, si de litteris sermo exoritur, vetera proferuntur, et nova; volant sententiae, verba resonant ampullosa. Praevenit interrogantem, non quaerenti respondet. Ipse quaerit, ipse solvit, et verba collocutoris imperfecta praescindit. Cum autem pulsato signo necesse est interrumpi colloquium, horam longam, breve queritur intervallum; quaerit licentiam, ut ad fabulas revertatur post horam, non ut quempiam aedificet, sed ut scientiam iactet. Aedificare potest, sed non aedificare intendit. Non curat te docere, vel a te doceri ipse quod nescit; sed ut scire sciatur quod scit. Quod si de religione agitur, statim visiones et somnia proferuntur. Denique laudat ieiunia, commendat vigilias, super omnia orationes exaltat; de patientia, de humilitate, et de singulis virtutibus plenissime, sed vanissime disputat: ut tu scilicet, si audieris, dicas, quod ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, et quia bonus homo de bono thesauro suo profert bona (Luc. VI, 43). Si ad ludicra sermo convertitur, in his quanto assuetior, tanto loquacior invenitur. Dicas, si audias rivum vanitatis, fluvium esse scurrilitatis os eius, ita ut severos quoque et graves animos in levitatem concitet risus. Et ut totum in brevi colligam, in multiloquio nota iactantiam. In hoc habes quartum gradum et descriptum, et nominatum. Fuge rem, et tene nomen. Hac eadem cautela iam accede ad quintum, quem nomino singularitatem.
english: But after vanity has begun to grow, and the bladder to swell, it is necessary that the windiness be belched through a wider hole, the fold being loosened, otherwise it will burst. So a monk, unseemly merriment overflowing, when he does not suffice to open it by laughter or signs, breaks out into the words of Elihu: “Behold my belly is as new wine without a vent, which bursts new bottles” (Job 32:19). He will therefore either speak, or burst. For he is full of words, and the spirit of his belly constrains him. He hungers and thirsts for hearers, to whom he may boast his vanities, to whom he may pour out all that he feels: to whom it may become known of what sort and how great he is. And when an occasion of speaking has been found, if the talk arises about letters, old things are brought forth, and new; sentences fly, swollen words resound. He anticipates the one asking, he answers the one not seeking. He himself asks, he himself solves, and he cuts off the imperfect words of his collocutor. But when, the signal having been struck, it is necessary that the conversation be interrupted, he complains of a long hour, a short interval; he seeks leave to return to fables after the hour, not that he may edify anyone, but that he may boast knowledge. He can edify, but he does not intend to edify. He does not care to teach you, or to be taught by you what he does not know; but that it may be known that he knows what he knows. And if religion is treated of, at once visions and dreams are brought forth. Finally he praises fasts, commends vigils, exalts prayers above all; he disputes most fully, but most vainly, about patience, about humility, and about each of the virtues: so that you, if you hear, may say that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and that a good man brings forth good things from his good treasure (Luke 6:45). If the talk is turned to sports, in these the more accustomed he is, the more talkative he is found. You would say, if you heard, that his mouth, a stream of vanity, is a river of scurrility, so that it stirs even severe and grave minds to the lightness of laughter. And that I may gather the whole in brief, note boasting in much speaking. In this you have the fourth step both described and named. Flee the thing, and keep the name. With this same caution now approach the fifth, which I name singularity.

Quod si de religione agitur, statim visiones et somnia proferuntur.
chunks.english: But when, the signal having been struck, it is necessary that the conversation be interrupted, he complains of a long hour, a short interval; he seeks leave to return to fables after the hour, not that he may edify anyone, but that he may boast knowledge. He can edify, but he does not intend to edify. He does not care to teach you, or to be taught by you what he does not know; but that it may be known that he knows what he knows.

chunks.latin: Denique laudat ieiunia, commendat vigilias, super omnia orationes exaltat; de patientia, de humilitate, et de singulis virtutibus plenissime, sed vanissime disputat: ut tu scilicet, si audieris, dicas, quod ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, et quia bonus homo de bono thesauro suo profert bona (Luc. VI, 43). Si ad ludicra sermo convertitur, in his quanto assuetior, tanto loquacior invenitur.
chunks.english: And if religion is treated of, at once visions and dreams are brought forth. Finally he praises fasts, commends vigils, exalts prayers above all; he disputes most fully, but most vainly, about patience, about humility, and about each of the virtues: so that you, if you hear, may say that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and that a good man brings forth good things from his good treasure (Luke 6:45). If the talk is turned to sports, in these the more accustomed he is, the more talkative he is found.

chunks.latin: Dicas, si audias rivum vanitatis, fluvium esse scurrilitatis os eius, ita ut severos quoque et graves animos in levitatem concitet risus. Et ut totum in brevi colligam, in multiloquio nota iactantiam. In hoc habes quartum gradum et descriptum, et nominatum. Fuge rem, et tene nomen. Hac eadem cautela iam accede ad quintum, quem nomino singularitatem.
chunks.english: You would say, if you heard, that his mouth, a stream of vanity, is a river of scurrility, so that it stirs even severe and grave minds to the lightness of laughter. And that I may gather the whole in brief, note boasting in much speaking. In this you have the fourth step both described and named. Flee the thing, and keep the name. With this same caution now approach the fifth, which I name singularity.

heading: CAPUT XIV. De quinto gradu superbiae, qui dicitur singularitas
latin: CAPUT XIV. De quinto gradu superbiae, qui dicitur singularitas.
english: Chapter XIV. On the fifth step of pride, which is called singularity.
label: CAPUT XIV. De quinto gradu superbiae, qui dicitur singularitas

chunks.latin: CAPUT XIV. De quinto gradu superbiae, qui dicitur singularitas.
chunks.english: Chapter XIV. On the fifth step of pride, which is called singularity.

latin: Turpe est ei, qui se supra caeteros iactat, si non plus caeteris aliquid agat, per quod ultra caeteros appareat. Proinde non sufficit ei quod communis monasterii regula, vel maiorum cohortantur exempla. Nec tamen melior esse studet, sed videri. Non melius vivere, sed videri vivere gestit, quatenus dicere possit: Non sum sicut caeteri hominum (Luc. XVIII, 11). Plus sibi blanditur de uno ieiunio, quod caeteris prandentibus facit, quam si cum caeteris septem dies ieiunaverit. Commodior sibi videtur una oratiuncula peculiaris, quam tota psalmodia unius noctis. Inter prandendum crebro solet oculos iactare per mensas, ut si quem minus comedere viderit, victum se doleat, et incipiat idipsum sibi crudeliter subtrahere, quod necessarium victui indulgendum praeviderat, plus gloriae metuens detrimentum, quam famis cruciatum. Si quem macriorem, si quem pallidiorem perspexerit, vilem se aestimat, nunquam requiescit. Et quoniam vultum ipse suum videre non potest, qualem scilicet se intuentibus offert, manus quas potest et brachia spectans, palpat costas, humeros attrectat et lumbos: ut secundum quod corporis sui membra, vel minus, vel satis exilia probat, pallorem oris ac colorem discernat. Ad omnia denique sua strenuus, ad communia piger. Vigilat in lecto, dormit in choro: cumque aliis psallentibus ad vigilias tota nocte dormitet, post vigilias aliis in claustro quiescentibus solus in oratorio remanet: exscreat, et tussit, gemitibus ac suspiriis aures foris sedentium de angulo implet. Cum autem ex his quae singulariter, sed inaniter agit, apud simpliciores eius opinio excreverit, qui profecto opera probant quae cernunt, sed unde prodeant non discernunt; dum miserum beatificant, in errorem inducunt (Isa. III, 12).
english: It is shameful for him who boasts himself above the rest, if he does not do something more than the rest, by which he may appear beyond the rest. Therefore what the common rule of the monastery, or the examples of the elders, urge, is not enough for him. Yet he does not strive to be better, but to be seen. He longs not to live better, but to be seen to live, so that he may say: “I am not as the rest of men” (Luke 18:11). He flatters himself more over one fast which he makes while the rest are dining, than if he had fasted seven days with the rest. One little private prayer seems to him more convenient than the whole psalmody of one night. At dinner he is accustomed frequently to cast his eyes over the tables, so that if he sees anyone eat less, he grieves to be beaten, and begins cruelly to withdraw from himself what he had foreseen should be granted as necessary for food, fearing more the loss of glory than the torment of hunger. If he has seen anyone thinner, anyone paler, he thinks himself cheap, he never rests. And because he cannot see his own face, what sort he offers to those looking on, looking at the hands and arms which he can, he feels his ribs, handles his shoulders and loins: so that according as he proves the members of his body either too little or sufficiently wasted, he may distinguish the paleness of his face and its color. In short, strenuous for all his own things, sluggish for common ones. He watches in bed, sleeps in choir: and when, while others are singing at vigils, he dozes the whole night, after vigils, while others rest in the cloister, he remains alone in the oratory: he hawks and coughs, and from a corner fills the ears of those sitting outside with groans and sighs. But when from these things which he does singularly but emptily his reputation has grown among the simpler, who indeed approve the works they see, but do not discern whence they proceed; while they call the wretch blessed, they lead him into error (Isa. 3:12).

heading: CAPUT XV. De sexto gradu superbiae, id est arrogantia
latin: CAPUT XV. De sexto gradu superbiae, id est arrogantia.
english: Chapter XV. On the sixth step of pride, that is arrogance.
label: CAPUT XV. De sexto gradu superbiae, id est arrogantia

chunks.latin: CAPUT XV. De sexto gradu superbiae, id est arrogantia.
chunks.english: Chapter XV. On the sixth step of pride, that is arrogance.

latin: Credit quod audit, laudat quod agit, et quod intendat non attendit. Obliviscitur intentionem dum amplectitur opinionem. Quique de omni alia re plus sibi credit, quam aliis, de se solo plus aliis credit, quam sibi: ut non iam verbo tenus, aut sola operum ostentatione suam praeferat religionem, sed intimo cordis credat affectu omnibus se sanctiorem: et quidquid de se laudatum agnoverit, non ignorantiae aut benevolentiae laudatoris, sed suis meritis arroganter ascribit. Unde post singularitatem, sextum sibi gradum iure arrogantia vindicat. Post hanc praesumptio invenitur, in qua septimus gradus constituitur.
english: He believes what he hears, he praises what he does, and he does not attend to what he intends. He forgets the intention while he embraces the opinion. And he who in every other matter believes himself more than others, about himself alone believes others more than himself: so that he no longer prefers his religion in word only, or by the mere display of works, but by the inmost affection of the heart believes himself holier than all: and whatever he has known to be praised in himself, he arrogantly ascribes not to the ignorance or goodwill of the praiser, but to his own merits. Whence after singularity, arrogance rightly claims the sixth step for itself. After this presumption is found, in which the seventh step is constituted.

heading: CAPUT XVI. De septimo gradu superbiae, qui est praesumptio
latin: CAPUT XVI. De septimo gradu superbiae, qui est praesumptio.
english: Chapter XVI. On the seventh step of pride, which is presumption.
label: CAPUT XVI. De septimo gradu superbiae, qui est praesumptio

chunks.latin: CAPUT XVI. De septimo gradu superbiae, qui est praesumptio.
chunks.english: Chapter XVI. On the seventh step of pride, which is presumption.

latin: Qui enim alios se praecellere putat, quomodo non plus de se, quam de aliis praesumat? Primus in conventibus residet, in consiliis primus respondet: non vocatus accedit, non iussus se intromittit: reordinat ordinata, reficit facta. Quidquid ipse non fecerit aut ordinaverit, nec recte factum, nec pulchre existimat ordinatum, Iudicat iudicantes, praeiudicat iudicaturis. Si, cum tempus advenerit, non promoveatur ad Prioratum; suum abbatem aut invidum iudicat, aut deceptum. Quod si mediocris ei aliqua obedientia iniuncta fuerit, indignatur, aspernatur, arbitrans se non esse minoribus occupandum, qui se ad maiora sentit idoneum. Sed qui sic promptulus ad omnia se magis temere, quam libere consuevit ingerere, impossibile est eum aliquando non errare. Ad praelatum autem pertinet errantem arguere. Sed quomodo culpam suam confitebitur, qui nec esse putat, nec putari culpabilis patitur? Propterea cum ei culpa imputatur, crescit, non amputatur. Si ergo cum argutus fuerit, declinare cor eius videris in verba malitiae, in octavum gradum, qui dicitur defensio peccatorum, noveris corruisse.
english: For he who thinks himself to excel others, how should he not presume more of himself than of others? He sits first in assemblies, he answers first in councils: uncalled he approaches, unbidden he intrudes: he reorders what has been ordered, he remakes what has been done. Whatever he himself has not done or ordered, he thinks neither rightly done nor beautifully ordered. He judges those who judge, he prejudges those about to judge. If, when the time has come, he is not promoted to the priorate, he judges his abbot either envious or deceived. But if some middling obedience is enjoined on him, he is indignant, he scorns it, thinking that he who feels himself fit for greater things is not to be occupied with lesser. But he who has been accustomed so readily to thrust himself into all things more rashly than freely, it is impossible that he should not at some time err. And it belongs to the prelate to rebuke the one erring. But how will he confess his fault, who neither thinks it is, nor suffers himself to be thought blameable? Therefore when a fault is imputed to him, it grows, it is not cut off. If then when he has been rebuked you see his heart decline into words of malice, know that he has fallen into the eighth step, which is called defense of sins.

heading: CAPUT XVII. De octavo gradu superbiae, qui est defensio peccatorum
latin: CAPUT XVII. De octavo gradu superbiae, qui est defensio peccatorum.
english: Chapter XVII. On the eighth step of pride, which is defense of sins.
label: CAPUT XVII. De octavo gradu superbiae, qui est defensio peccatorum

chunks.latin: CAPUT XVII. De octavo gradu superbiae, qui est defensio peccatorum.
chunks.english: Chapter XVII. On the eighth step of pride, which is defense of sins.

latin: Multis vero modis fiunt excusationes in peccatis. Aut enim dicit qui se excusat, Non feci; aut, Feci quidem, sed bene feci; aut, Si male, non multum male; aut, Si multum male, non mala intentione. Si autem et de illa, sicut Adam vel Eva, convincitur, aliena suasione excusare se nititur. Sed qui procaciter etiam aperta defendit, quando occultas et malas cogitationes, cordi suo advenientes, humiliter revelaret abbati?
english: Now excuses in sins are made in many ways. For either he who excuses himself says, “I did not do it”; or, “I did it, but I did well”; or, “If badly, not very badly”; or, “If very badly, not with a bad intention.” And if he is convicted even of that, like Adam or Eve, he tries to excuse himself by another’s persuasion. But he who shamelessly defends even open things, when would he humbly reveal to the abbot the hidden and evil thoughts coming to his heart?

heading: CAPUT XVIII. De nono gradu superbiae, qui est simulata confessio
latin: CAPUT XVIII. De nono gradu superbiae, qui est simulata confessio.
english: Chapter XVIII. On the ninth step of pride, which is feigned confession.
label: CAPUT XVIII. De nono gradu superbiae, qui est simulata confessio

chunks.latin: CAPUT XVIII. De nono gradu superbiae, qui est simulata confessio.
chunks.english: Chapter XVIII. On the ninth step of pride, which is feigned confession.

latin: Licet vero genera haec excusationis eatenus mala iudicentur, quatenus ore prophetico verba malitiae appellantur (Psal. CXL, 4); multo tamen periculosior est fallax ac superba confessio, quam pervicax et obstinata defensio. Nonnulli enim cum de apertioribus arguuntur, scientes quod si se defenderent, sibi non crederetur, subtilius inveniunt argumentum defensionis, verba respondentes dolosae confessionis. Est quippe, ut scriptum est, qui nequiter humiliat se, et interiora eius plena sunt dolo (Eccli. XIX, 23). Vultus demittitur, prosternitur corpus: aliquas sibi lacrymulas extorquent, si possunt; vocem suspiriis, verba gemitibus interrumpunt. Nec solum qui eiusmodi est, obiecta non excusat, sed ipse quoque culpam exaggerat: ut dum impossibile aliquid aut incredibile culpae suae ore ipsius additum audis, etiam illud, quod ratum putabas, discredere possis; et ex eo quod falsum esse non dubitas dum confitetur, in dubium veniat quod quasi certum tenebatur. Dumque affirmant quod credi nolunt, confitendo culpam defendunt, et aperiendo tegunt; quando et confessio laudabiliter sonat in ore, et adhuc iniquitas occultatur in corde: quatenus magis ex humilitate quam ex veritate confiteri putet qui audit, aptans eis illud Scripturae: Iustus in principio sermonis accusator est sui (Prov. XVIII, 17). Malunt enim apud homines veritate periclitari, quam humilitate, cum apud Deum periclitentur utrinque. Aut si adeo culpa manifesta sit quod nulla penitus versutia tegi possit; nihilominus tamen vocem, non cor poenitentis assumunt, qua notam, non culpam deleant, dum ignorantiam manifestae transgressionis, decore recompensant publicae confessionis.
english: And though these kinds of excuse are judged evil to this extent, that they are called by the prophetic mouth words of malice (Ps. 140:4); yet far more dangerous is a false and proud confession than a stubborn and obstinate defense. For some, when they are rebuked for more open things, knowing that if they defended themselves they would not be believed, find a subtler argument of defense, answering with words of a deceitful confession. For there is, as it is written, one who wickedly humbles himself, and his inward parts are full of deceit (Sir. 19:23). The face is cast down, the body is prostrated: they wring out some little tears for themselves, if they can; they interrupt the voice with sighs, the words with groans. And not only does one of this sort not excuse what is objected, but he himself also exaggerates the fault: so that when you hear something impossible or incredible added to his fault by his own mouth, you may disbelieve even that which you thought established; and from that which you do not doubt is false while he confesses, that which was held as almost certain may come into doubt. And while they affirm what they do not wish to be believed, by confessing they defend the fault, and by opening they cover it; so that the confession sounds praiseworthily in the mouth, and iniquity is still hidden in the heart: so that he who hears may think them to confess more from humility than from truth, applying to them that of Scripture: “The just man is the accuser of himself in the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). For they prefer to be in peril among men as to truth rather than as to humility, while before God they are in peril on both sides. Or if the fault is so manifest that no cunning can cover it; nevertheless they assume the voice, not the heart, of one penitent, that they may wipe out the mark, not the fault, while they compensate the ignorance of an open transgression with the decoration of a public confession.

chunks.latin: Dumque affirmant quod credi nolunt, confitendo culpam defendunt, et aperiendo tegunt; quando et confessio laudabiliter sonat in ore, et adhuc iniquitas occultatur in corde: quatenus magis ex humilitate quam ex veritate confiteri putet qui audit, aptans eis illud Scripturae: Iustus in principio sermonis accusator est sui (Prov. XVIII, 17).
chunks.english: And while they affirm what they do not wish to be believed, by confessing they defend the fault, and by opening they cover it; so that the confession sounds praiseworthily in the mouth, and iniquity is still hidden in the heart: so that he who hears may think them to confess more from humility than from truth, applying to them that of Scripture: “The just man is the accuser of himself in the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17).

chunks.latin: Malunt enim apud homines veritate periclitari, quam humilitate, cum apud Deum periclitentur utrinque. Aut si adeo culpa manifesta sit quod nulla penitus versutia tegi possit; nihilominus tamen vocem, non cor poenitentis assumunt, qua notam, non culpam deleant, dum ignorantiam manifestae transgressionis, decore recompensant publicae confessionis.
chunks.english: For they prefer to be in peril among men as to truth rather than as to humility, while before God they are in peril on both sides. Or if the fault is so manifest that no cunning can cover it; nevertheless they assume the voice, not the heart, of one penitent, that they may wipe out the mark, not the fault, while they compensate the ignorance of an open transgression with the decoration of a public confession.

latin: Gloriosa res humilitas, qua ipsa quoque superbia palliare se appetit, ne vilescat! Sed haec cito tergiversatio a praelato deprehenditur, si ad hanc superbam humilitatem non leviter flectitur, quo magis dissimulat culpam, vel differat poenam. Vasa figuli probat fornax, et tribulatio vere poenitentes discernit. Qui enim veraciter poenitet, laborem poenitentiae non abhorret: sed quidquid sibi pro culpa quam odit iniungitur, tacita conscientia patienter amplectitur. In ipsa quoque obedientia duris ac contrariis rebus obortis, quibuslibet irrogatis iniuriis sustinens non lassescit, ut in quarto gradu se stare indicet humilitatis. Cuius vero simulata confessio est, una vel levi contumelia, aut exigua poena interrogatus, iam humilitatem simulare, iam simulationem dissimulare non potest. Murmurat, frendet, irascitur; nec in quarto stare humilitatis, sed in nonum superbiae gradum corruisse probatur, qui secundum quod descriptus est, recte simulata confessio appellari potest. Quanta putas tunc confusio sit in corde superbi cum fraus decipitur, pax amittitur, laus minuitur, nec culpa diluitur? Tandem notatur ab omnibus, iudicatur ab omnibus: eoque vehementius omnes indignantur, quo falsum conspiciunt quidquid de eo prius opinabantur. Tunc opus est praelato, ut eo minus illi parcendum putet, quo magis omnes offenderet, si uni parcere.
english: Glorious is humility, with which even pride itself desires to cloak itself, lest it become cheap! But this tergiversation is quickly detected by the prelate, if he is not lightly bent to this proud humility, by which the more he disguises the fault, or puts off the punishment. The furnace proves the vessels of the potter, and tribulation discerns those truly penitent. For he who truly repents does not shrink from the labor of penitence: but whatever is enjoined on him for the fault which he hates, he embraces patiently with a silent conscience. In that obedience also, when hard and contrary things arise, and whatever injuries are inflicted, he does not grow weary in bearing, so as to show that he stands in the fourth step of humility. But he whose confession is feigned, when asked with one or a light insult, or a small punishment, can no longer feign humility, no longer disguise the feigning. He murmurs, he gnashes, he is angry; and he is proved not to stand in the fourth of humility, but to have fallen into the ninth step of pride, which, according as it has been described, can rightly be called feigned confession. How great do you think is then the confusion in the heart of the proud man, when the fraud is detected, peace is lost, praise is lessened, and the fault is not washed away? At last he is noted by all, judged by all: and all are the more vehemently indignant, the more they see to be false whatever they had formerly thought of him. Then it is necessary for the prelate to think him the less to be spared, the more he would offend all if he spared one.

heading: CAPUT XIX. De decimo gradu superbiae, qui est rebellio
latin: CAPUT XIX. De decimo gradu superbiae, qui est rebellio.
english: Chapter XIX. On the tenth step of pride, which is rebellion.
label: CAPUT XIX. De decimo gradu superbiae, qui est rebellio

chunks.latin: CAPUT XIX. De decimo gradu superbiae, qui est rebellio.
chunks.english: Chapter XIX. On the tenth step of pride, which is rebellion.

latin: Hic nisi eum miseratio superna respiciat, (quod valde difficile talibus est) universorum iudiciis tacitus acquiescat; frontosus mox et impudens factus, tanto deterius, quanto desperatius in decimum gradum per rebellionem corruit: quippe prius latenter arrogans fratres contempserat, iam patenter inobediens etiam magistrum contemnit.
english: Here, unless heavenly pity look upon him (which is very difficult for such), he may silently acquiesce in the judgments of all; made soon shameless and impudent, so much the worse as more despairingly he falls by rebellion into the tenth step: for whereas before, arrogantly in secret, he had despised the brothers, now openly disobedient he despises even the master.

chunks.latin: Hic nisi eum miseratio superna respiciat, (quod valde difficile talibus est) universorum iudiciis tacitus acquiescat; frontosus mox et impudens factus, tanto deterius, quanto desperatius in decimum gradum per rebellionem corruit: quippe prius latenter arrogans fratres contempserat, iam patenter inobediens etiam magistrum contemnit.

latin: Sciendum autem est, quod omnes gradus, quos in duodecim partitus sum, in tres tantummodo colligi possunt: ut in sex superioribus contemptus fratrum, in quatuor sequentibus contemptus magistri, in duobus, qui restant, consummetur contemptus Dei. Notandum quoque, quod hi duo superbiae gradus ultimi, qui et humilitatis ascendendo primi inveniuntur; sicut extra congregationem ascendendi sunt, ita in congregatione descendi non possunt. Quod autem ante ascendi debeant, ex hoc aperte datur intelligi, quod de tertio gradu in Regula legitur: «Tertius,» inquit, «gradus est, ut quis pro Dei amore omni obedientia se subdat maiori.» (Regul. 7, 31.) Si ergo in tertio gradu subiectio collocatur, quae procul dubio fit, quando novitius primum conventui sociatur; consequens est, quod duo iam anteriores transcensi intelligantur. Denique ubi fratrum concordiam, et magistri sententiam monachus spernit, quid ultra in monasterio, nisi scandalum facit?
english: And it is to be known that all the steps which I have divided into twelve can be gathered into three only: so that in the six higher there is contempt of the brothers, in the four following contempt of the master, in the two that remain the contempt of God is completed. It is also to be noted that these two last steps of pride, which in climbing are also the first of humility, as they are to be climbed outside the congregation, so they cannot be descended in the congregation. And that they ought to be climbed before is openly given to be understood from this, that of the third step it is read in the Rule: “The third,” it says, “step is, that one for the love of God subject himself in all obedience to a greater.” (Rule 7.31.) If therefore in the third step subjection is placed, which beyond doubt takes place when a novice is first associated with the convent, it follows that the two former are already understood to have been passed. Finally, when a monk despises the concord of the brothers and the sentence of the master, what does he do further in the monastery, except make scandal?

heading: CAPUT XX. De undecimo gradu superbiae, qui est libertas peccandi
latin: CAPUT XX. De undecimo gradu superbiae, qui est libertas peccandi.
english: Chapter XX. On the eleventh step of pride, which is liberty of sinning.
label: CAPUT XX. De undecimo gradu superbiae, qui est libertas peccandi

chunks.latin: CAPUT XX. De undecimo gradu superbiae, qui est libertas peccandi.
chunks.english: Chapter XX. On the eleventh step of pride, which is liberty of sinning.

latin: Post decimum itaque gradum, qui rebellio dictus est, expulsus vel egressus de monasterio statim excipitur ab undecimo. Et tunc ingreditur vias, quae videntur hominibus bonae, quarum finis (nisi forte Deus eas illi sepierit) demerget eum in profundum inferni, id est in contemptum Dei. Impius siquidem cum venerit in profundum malorum, contemnit (Prov. XVIII, 3). Potest autem undecimus gradus appellari libertas peccandi, per quam monachus, cum iam nec magistrum videt quem timeat, nec fratres quos revereatur, tanto securius, quanto liberius sua desideria implere delectatur, a quibus in monasterio tam pudore, quam timore prohibebatur. Sed etsi iam vel fratres, vel abbatem non timet, nondum tamen Dei penitus formidine caret. Hanc ratio, tenuiter adhuc submurmurans, voluntati proponit, nec sine aliqua dubitatione quaeque primum illicita perficit; sed, sicut is qui vadum tentat, pedetentim, non cursim vitiorum gurgitem intrat.
english: After the tenth step, then, which has been called rebellion, one expelled or gone out from the monastery is at once received by the eleventh. And then he enters ways that seem good to men, whose end (unless perhaps God hedge them for him) will plunge him into the depth of hell, that is into contempt of God. For the impious, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises (Prov. 18:3). And the eleventh step can be called liberty of sinning, by which a monk, when he now neither sees a master whom he may fear, nor brothers whom he may revere, delights so much the more securely, as more freely, to fulfill his desires, from which in the monastery he was restrained as much by shame as by fear. But although he now fears neither the brothers nor the abbot, he has not yet wholly lost the fear of God. Reason, still faintly murmuring, sets this before the will, and not without some hesitation he first accomplishes unlawful things; but, like one who tries a ford, he enters the whirlpool of vices step by step, not at a run.

heading: CAPUT XXI. De duodecimo gradu superbiae, qui est consuetudo peccandi
latin: CAPUT XXI. De duodecimo gradu superbiae, qui est consuetudo peccandi.
english: Chapter XXI. On the twelfth step of pride, which is the habit of sinning.
label: CAPUT XXI. De duodecimo gradu superbiae, qui est consuetudo peccandi

chunks.latin: CAPUT XXI. De duodecimo gradu superbiae, qui est consuetudo peccandi.
chunks.english: Chapter XXI. On the twelfth step of pride, which is the habit of sinning.

latin: At postquam terribili Dei iudicio prima flagitia impunitas sequitur, experta voluptas libenter repetitur, repetita blanditur. Concupiscentia reviviscente sopitur ratio, ligat consuetudo. Trahitur miser in profundum malorum, traditur captivus tyrannidi vitiorum, ita ut carnalium voragine desideriorum absorptus, suae rationis divinique timoris oblitus, dicat insipiens in corde suo: Non est Deus (Psal. XIII, 1). Iam indifferenter libitis pro licitis utitur, iam ab illicitis cogitandis, patrandis, investigandis animus, manus, vel pedes non prohibentur: sed quidquid in cor, in buccam, ad manum venerit, machinatur, garrit et operatur, malevolus, vaniloquus, facinorosus. Quemadmodum denique ascensis his omnibus gradibus, corde iam alacri et absque labore pro bona consuetudine iustus currit ad vitam: sic descensis impius eisdem, pro malo usu non ratione se gubernans, non timoris freno retentans, intrepidus festinat ad mortem. Medii sunt qui fatigantur, angustiantur: qui nunc metu cruciantur gehennae, nunc pristina retardati consuetudine, descendendo vel ascendendo laborant. Supremus tantum et infimus currunt absque impedimento, et absque labore. Ad mortem hic, ad vitam ille festinat; alter alacrior, alter proclivior. Illum alacrem caritas, hunc proclivem cupiditas facit. In altero amor, in altero stupor laborem non sentit. In illo denique perfecta caritas, in isto consummata iniquitas foras mittit timorem. Illi veritas, huic caecitas dat securitatem. Potest ergo duodecimus gradus appellari consuetudo peccandi, qua Dei metus amittitur, contemptus incurritur.
english: But after, by the terrible judgment of God, impunity follows the first crimes, the pleasure experienced is gladly repeated, the repeated flatters. With concupiscence reviving, reason is lulled, habit binds. The wretch is drawn into the depth of evils, is delivered captive to the tyranny of vices, so that, swallowed in the gulf of carnal desires, forgetful of his own reason and of the fear of God, the fool says in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1). Now he uses the pleasant indifferently for the lawful; now mind, hands, or feet are not forbidden from thinking, doing, seeking the unlawful: but whatever has come into the heart, into the mouth, to the hand, he devises, chatters, and works, malevolent, vain-speaking, criminal. As finally, when all these steps have been climbed, the just man, with a heart now eager and without labor by good habit, runs to life: so the impious, having descended the same, not governing himself by reason, not holding himself by the bridle of fear, for an evil use, hastens fearlessly to death. Those in the middle are they who are wearied, distressed: who now are tortured by fear of hell, now, delayed by former habit, labor in descending or ascending. Only the highest and the lowest run without hindrance and without labor. This one hastens to death, that one to life; the one more eager, the other more downhill. Charity makes that one eager, cupidity makes this one downhill. In the one love, in the other stupor, does not feel labor. In that one, finally, perfect charity, in this one consummated iniquity, casts out fear. To the one truth, to the other blindness, gives security. The twelfth step, then, can be called the habit of sinning, by which the fear of God is lost, contempt is incurred.

heading: CAPUT XXII. An et quomodo orandum pro desperatis, et mortuis secundum animam
latin: CAPUT XXII. An et quomodo orandum pro desperatis, et mortuis secundum animam.
english: Chapter XXII. Whether and how one should pray for the desperate, and for those dead according to the soul.
label: CAPUT XXII. An et quomodo orandum pro desperatis, et mortuis secundum animam

chunks.latin: CAPUT XXII. An et quomodo orandum pro desperatis, et mortuis secundum animam.
chunks.english: Chapter XXII. Whether and how one should pray for the desperate, and for those dead according to the soul.

latin: Pro tali iam, inquit Ioannes apostolus, non dico ut quis oret (I Ioan. V, 16). Sed nunquid dicis, o Apostole, ut quis desperet? Imo gemat qui illum amat. Non praesumat orare, nec desistat plorare. Quid est quod dico? An forte ullum remanet spei refugium, ubi oratio non invenit locum? Audi credentem, audi sperantem, nec tamen orantem. Domine, inquit, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus. Magna fides, qua credidit sua praesentia Dominum nortem prohibere potuisse si adfuisset. Modo autem quid? Absit ut quem credidit vivum potuisse servare, mortuum dubitet posse resuscitare. Sed nunc, inquit, scio quia quaecunque poposceris a Deo, dabit tibi Deus. Deinde quaerenti ubi posuissent eum, respondet: Veni, et vide. Quamobrem? O Martha, magna nobis tuae fidei insignia tribuis: sed quomodo cum tanta fide diffidis? Veni, inquis, et vide. Cur et, si non desperas, non sequeris, et dicis, Et resuscita? si autem desperas, cur Magistrum sine causa fatigas? An forte fides aliquando recipit, quod oratio non praesumit? Denique appropinquantem cadaveri prohibes, et dicis: Domine, iam fetet; quatriduanus enim est (Ioan. XI, 21, 22, 34, 39). Desperando dicis hoc, an dissimulando? Sic quippe ipse Dominus post resurrectionem finxit se longius ire (Luc. XXIV, 28), cum mallet cum discipulis remanere. O sanctae mulieres Christi familiares, si fratrem vestrum amatis, cur eius misericordiam non flagitatis, de cuius potentia dubitare, pietate diffidere non potetis? Respondent: Sic melius tanquam non orantes oramus, sic efficacius tanquam diffidentes confidimus. Exhibemus fidem, perhibemus affectum: scit ipse, cui non est opus ut aliquid dicatur, quid desideremus. Scimus quidem quod omnia potest: sed hoc tam grande miraculum, tam novum, tam inauditum, etsi eius subest potentiae, multum tamen excedit universa merita humilitatis nostrae. Sufficit nobis potentiae locum, pietati dedisse occasionem; malentes patienter exspectare quid velit quam impudenter quaerere quod forsitan nolit. Denique quod nostris meritis deest, verecundia fortasse supplebit. Petri quoque post gravem lapsum lacrymam quidem video, sed precem non audio: nec tamen de indulgentia dubito.
english: “For such a one already,” says the apostle John, “I do not say that anyone should pray” (1 John 5:16). But do you say, O Apostle, that anyone should despair? Rather let him groan who loves him. Let him not presume to pray, nor let him cease to weep. What is it that I say? Does any refuge of hope perhaps remain, where prayer finds no place? Hear one believing, hear one hoping, and yet not praying. “Lord,” she says, “if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Great faith, by which she believed that the Lord’s presence could have forbidden death if He had been there. But now what? Far be it that she should doubt that He whom she believed could keep the living, can raise the dead. “But now,” she says, “I know that whatever You ask of God, God will give You.” Then to Him asking where they had laid him, she answers: “Come and see.” Why? O Martha, you give us great marks of your faith: but how, with so great a faith, do you distrust? “Come,” you say, “and see.” Why also, if you do not despair, do you not follow, and say, “And raise him”? If you do despair, why do you weary the Master without cause? Or does faith sometimes receive what prayer does not presume? Finally you forbid Him approaching the corpse, and say: “Lord, already he stinks; for he is four days dead” (John 11:21, 22, 34, 39). Do you say this despairing, or dissembling? For so the Lord Himself after the resurrection pretended that He would go farther (Luke 24:28), when He preferred to remain with the disciples. O holy women, familiars of Christ, if you love your brother, why do you not beg His mercy, of whose power you cannot doubt, of whose piety you cannot distrust? They answer: So we pray better as if not praying, so we trust more effectively as if distrusting. We show faith, we bear witness to affection: He knows, to whom it is not needful that anything be said, what we desire. We know indeed that He can do all things: but this so great a miracle, so new, so unheard of, even if it lies within His power, yet greatly exceeds all the merits of our humility. It is enough for us to have given a place to power, an occasion to piety; preferring patiently to wait for what He wills rather than shamelessly to seek what perhaps He does not will. Finally what our merits lack, shame perhaps will supply. In Peter also, after a heavy fall, I see a tear, but I do not hear a prayer: nor yet do I doubt of pardon.

chunks.latin: Pro tali iam, inquit Ioannes apostolus, non dico ut quis oret (I Ioan. V, 16). Sed nunquid dicis, o Apostole, ut quis desperet? Imo gemat qui illum amat. Non praesumat orare, nec desistat plorare. Quid est quod dico? An forte ullum remanet spei refugium, ubi oratio non invenit locum? Audi credentem, audi sperantem, nec tamen orantem. Domine, inquit, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus.
chunks.english: “For such a one already,” says the apostle John, “I do not say that anyone should pray” (1 John 5:16). But do you say, O Apostle, that anyone should despair? Rather let him groan who loves him. Let him not presume to pray, nor let him cease to weep. What is it that I say? Does any refuge of hope perhaps remain, where prayer finds no place? Hear one believing, hear one hoping, and yet not praying.

chunks.latin: Magna fides, qua credidit sua praesentia Dominum nortem prohibere potuisse si adfuisset. Modo autem quid? Absit ut quem credidit vivum potuisse servare, mortuum dubitet posse resuscitare. Sed nunc, inquit, scio quia quaecunque poposceris a Deo, dabit tibi Deus. Deinde quaerenti ubi posuissent eum, respondet: Veni, et vide. Quamobrem? O Martha, magna nobis tuae fidei insignia tribuis: sed quomodo cum tanta fide diffidis? Veni, inquis, et vide.
chunks.english: “Lord,” she says, “if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Great faith, by which she believed that the Lord’s presence could have forbidden death if He had been there. Denique appropinquantem cadaveri prohibes, et dicis: Domine, iam fetet; quatriduanus enim est (Ioan. XI, 21, 22, 34, 39). Desperando dicis hoc, an dissimulando?

latin: Disce et in Matre Domini magnam in mirabilibus fidem habere, in magna fide verecundiam retinere. Disce verecundia decorare fidem, reprimere praesumptionem. Vinum, inquit, non habent (Ioan. II, 3). Quam breviter, quam reverenter suggessit, unde pie fuit sollicita! Et ut discas in huiusmodi magis pie gemere, quam petere praesumptuose; pietatis aestum pudoris temperans umbra, conceptam precis fiduciam verecunde suppressit. Non frontose accessit, non palam locuta est, ut audacter coram omnibus diceret: Obsecro, fili, deficit vinum, contristantur convivae, confunditur sponsus; ostende quid possis. Sed licet haec aut multo plura pectus aestuans, fervens loqueretur affectus; privatim tamen potentem pia Filium mater adiit, non potentiam tentans, sed voluntatem explorans. Vinum, inquit, non habent. Quid modestius? quid fidelius? Non defuit pietati fides, voci gravitas, efficacia voto. Si ergo illa, cum mater sit, sese matrem oblita non audet petere miraculum vini; ego vile mancipium, cui permagnum est Filii simul ac Matris esse vernaculum, qua fronte praesumo pro vita petere quatriduani?
english: Learn also in the Mother of the Lord to have a great faith in wonders, to keep shame in a great faith. Learn by shame to adorn faith, to check presumption. “They have no wine,” she says (John 2:3). How briefly, how reverently she suggested that of which she was piously anxious! And that you may learn in such things rather to groan piously than to ask presumptuously; the shade of modesty tempering the heat of piety, she bashfully suppressed the conceived confidence of a prayer. She did not approach boldly, she did not speak openly, so as to say audaciously before all: “I beseech You, son, the wine fails, the guests are sad, the bridegroom is confounded; show what You can.” But though this, or much more, a burning breast, a fervent affection, would speak; yet privately the pious mother approached her powerful Son, not testing power, but exploring the will. “They have no wine,” she says. What more modest? What more faithful? Faith was not lacking to piety, gravity to the voice, efficacy to the wish. If then she, though she is mother, forgetting herself as mother, does not dare to ask the miracle of wine: I, a cheap servant, to whom it is a great thing to be a household servant of the Son and of the Mother together, with what face do I presume to ask life for one four days dead?

latin: Duo etiam in Evangelio caeci visum, alter accepisse, alter recepisse leguntur: alter quem amiserat, alter quem nunquam habuerat; unus scilicet excaecatus, alter caecus natus. Sed qui excaecatus, miserabilibus mirisque clamoribus miram misericordiam meruit: qui vero caecus natus, tanto misericordius, quanto mirabilius nullis suis precibus praeventum sui illuminatoris beneficium nihilominus sensit. Illi denique dictum est, Fides tua te salvum fecit: huic autem non (Luc. XVIII, 35-43; Ioan. IX). Duos quoque recenter mortuos, tertium iam quatriduanum, lego resuscitatos: solam tamen Archisynagogi filiam, in domo adhuc positam, precibus patris; duos autem ex insperata magnitudine pietatis (Marc. V, 35-42; Luc. VII, 11-15; Ioan. XI).
english: Two also in the Gospel are read to have received sight, the one to have accepted it, the other to have recovered it: the one what he had lost, the other what he had never had; one namely blinded, the other born blind. But he who was blinded merited a wondrous mercy by miserable and wondrous cries: but he who was born blind felt no less, so much the more mercifully as more wondrously, the benefit of his enlightener, not anticipated by any prayers of his own. To the former, finally, it was said, “Your faith has saved you”: but not to this one (Luke 18:35–43; John 9). Two also recently dead, a third already four days, I read raised: yet only the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, still placed in the house, by the prayers of her father; but the two from the unhoped-for greatness of piety (Mark 5:35–42; Luke 7:11–15; John 11).

latin: Simili etiam forma si contigerit (quod Deus avertat) aliquem de fratribus nostris, non in corpore, sed in anima mori; quandiu adhuc inter nos erit, pulsabo et ego meis qualiscunque peccator, pulsabo et fratrum precibus Salvatorem. Si revixerit, lucrati erimus fratrem: sin vero non mereamur exaudiri, ubi iam vel tolerare vivos, vel tolerari a vivis non poterit, sed incipiet efferri, semper quidem fideliter gemo, sed iam non ita fiducialiter oro. Non aperte audeo dicere, Veni, Domine, suscita mortuum nostrum: corde tamen suspenso, tremulus intus clamare non cesso, Si forte, si forte, si forte desiderium pauperum exaudiet Dominus, praeparationem cordis eorum audiet auris eius; et illud, Nunquid mortuis facies mirabilia, aut medici suscitabunt, et confitebuntur tibi? et de quatriduano: Nunquid narrabit aliquis in sepulcro misericordiam tuam, et veritatem tuam in perditione? (Psal. LXXXVII, 11, 12.) Potest interim Salvator, si vult, insperate et improvise occurrere nobis, lacrymisque portantium motus, non precibus, mortui vitam reddere vivis, aut certe iam sepultum revocare a mortuis. Mortuum autem dixerim illum, qui sua peccata defendens, in octavum iam corruit gradum. A mortuo enim, tanquam qui non est, perit confessio (Eccli. XVII, 26). Post decimum vero, qui tertius est ab octavo, iam effertur in libertatem peccandi, quando expellitur a consortio monasterii. At postquam quartum transierit, iam recte quatriduanus dicitur, dum in quintum decidens per consuetudinem sepelitur.
english: In a like form also, if it should happen (which God avert) that one of our brothers should die, not in body but in soul; so long as he is still among us, I also, such a sinner as I am, will knock, I will knock also with the prayers of the brothers upon the Savior. If he comes to life, we shall have gained a brother: but if we do not deserve to be heard, when he can no longer either bear the living or be borne by the living, but begins to be carried out, I always indeed groan faithfully, but I no longer pray so trustingly. I do not dare to say openly, “Come, Lord, raise our dead”: yet with a suspended heart I do not cease to cry within, trembling, “If perhaps, if perhaps, if perhaps the Lord will hear the desire of the poor, His ear will hear the preparation of their heart”; and that, “Will You do wonders for the dead, or shall physicians raise them, and they confess to You?” and of the four-days-dead: “Shall anyone tell Your mercy in the grave, and Your truth in destruction?” (Ps. 87:11–12.) The Savior can meanwhile, if He wills, meet us unhoped and unforeseen, and moved by the tears of those carrying, not by prayers, restore the life of the dead to the living, or even already buried call him back from the dead. And I would call him dead who, defending his own sins, has already fallen into the eighth step. For from the dead, as from one who is not, confession perishes (Sir. 17:26). But after the tenth, which is the third from the eighth, he is already carried out into the liberty of sinning, when he is expelled from the company of the monastery. And after he has passed the fourth, he is already rightly called four days dead, while falling into the fifth he is buried by habit.

latin: Absit autem a nobis, ut etiam pro talibus, etsi palam non praesumimus, vel in cordibus nostris orare cessemus: cum Paulus eos quoque lugeret, quos sine poenitentia mortuos sciret (II Cor. XII, 21). Etsi enim a communibus orationibus ipsi se excludunt, sed ab affectibus omnino non possunt. Viderint tamen in quanto periculo sint, pro quibus Ecclesia palam orare non audeat, quae fidenter etiam pro Iudaeis, pro haereticis, pro Gentilibus orat. Cum enim in Parasceve nominatim oretur pro quibuslibet malis, nulla tamen mentio fit de excommunicatis.
english: But far be it from us that even for such, though we do not presume openly, we should cease to pray even in our hearts: since Paul also mourned those whom he knew to have died without penitence (2 Cor. 12:21). For though they exclude themselves from common prayers, they cannot wholly from affections. Yet let them see in how great peril they are, for whom the Church does not dare to pray openly, who prays confidently even for Jews, for heretics, for Gentiles. For while on Good Friday prayer is made by name for any evils whatsoever, yet no mention is made of the excommunicated.

latin: Dicis forte, frater Godefride, me aliud quam tu quaesisti, et quam ipse promisi, tandem exhibuisse, cum pro gradibus humilitatis, superbiae gradus videar descripsisse. Ad quod ego: Non potui docere nisi quod didici. Non putavi congruum me describere ascensiones, qui plus descendere, quam ascendere novi. Proponat tibi beatus Benedictus gradus humilitatis, quos ipse prius in corde suo disposuit: ego quid proponam non habeo, nisi ordinem meae descensionis. In quo tamen, si diligenter inspicitur, via forsitan ascensionis reperitur. Si enim tibi Romam tendenti homo inde veniens obviaret, quaesitus viam, quid melius quam illam, qua venit, ostenderet? Dum castella, villas, urbes, fluvios, ac montes, per quos transierit, nominat, suum denuntians iter, tuum tibi praenuntiat: ita ut eadem loca recognoscas eundo, quae ille pertransiit veniendo. In hac similiter nostra descensione gradus ascensorios fortasse reperies, quos ascendendo melius tu in tuo corde, quam in nostro codice leges. Amen.
english: You say perhaps, brother Godfrey, that I have at last exhibited something other than you asked, and than I myself promised, since instead of the steps of humility I seem to have described the steps of pride. To which I: I could not teach except what I have learned. I did not think it fitting that I should describe ascents, who know how to descend more than to ascend. Let blessed Benedict set before you the steps of humility, which he first arranged in his own heart: I have nothing to set forth except the order of my own descent. In which nevertheless, if it is diligently looked into, the way of ascent is perhaps found. For if a man coming from there met you as you were going to Rome, and being asked the way, what better could he show than that by which he came? While he names the castles, villages, cities, rivers, and mountains through which he has passed, announcing his own journey, he foretells yours to you: so that you recognize in going the same places which he passed through in coming. In this descent of ours likewise you will perhaps find the ascending steps, which in climbing you will read better in your own heart than in our book. Amen.

chunks.latin: Dicis forte, frater Godefride, me aliud quam tu quaesisti, et quam ipse promisi, tandem exhibuisse, cum pro gradibus humilitatis, superbiae gradus videar descripsisse. Ad quod ego: Non potui docere nisi quod didici. Non putavi congruum me describere ascensiones, qui plus descendere, quam ascendere novi. Proponat tibi beatus Benedictus gradus humilitatis, quos ipse prius in corde suo disposuit: ego quid proponam non habeo, nisi ordinem meae descensionis. In quo tamen, si diligenter inspicitur, via forsitan ascensionis reperitur.
chunks.english: You say perhaps, brother Godfrey, that I have at last exhibited something other than you asked, and than I myself promised, since instead of the steps of humility I seem to have described the steps of pride. To which I: I could not teach except what I have learned. I did not think it fitting that I should describe ascents, who know how to descend more than to ascend. Let blessed Benedict set before you the steps of humility, which he first arranged in his own heart: I have nothing to set forth except the order of my own descent.

chunks.latin: Si enim tibi Romam tendenti homo inde veniens obviaret, quaesitus viam, quid melius quam illam, qua venit, ostenderet? Dum castella, villas, urbes, fluvios, ac montes, per quos transierit, nominat, suum denuntians iter, tuum tibi praenuntiat: ita ut eadem loca recognoscas eundo, quae ille pertransiit veniendo. In hac similiter nostra descensione gradus ascensorios fortasse reperies, quos ascendendo melius tu in tuo corde, quam in nostro codice leges. Amen.
chunks.english: In which nevertheless, if it is diligently looked into, the way of ascent is perhaps found. For if a man coming from there met you as you were going to Rome, and being asked the way, what better could he show than that by which he came? While he names the castles, villages, cities, rivers, and mountains through which he has passed, announcing his own journey, he foretells yours to you: so that you recognize in going the same places which he passed through in coming. In this descent of ours likewise you will perhaps find the ascending steps, which in climbing you will read better in your own heart than in our book. Amen.
